What's tested
  • Terms: occlusion vs articulation, neutral zone, occlusal plane, curves of Spee and Wilson, compensating curve, sphere of Monson, crossbite
  • MIP vs centric occlusion vs centric relation (the exam uses CO only to mean "teeth touching with the joints seated")
  • Angle classes, cusp-fossa vs cusp-marginal ridge, and "what cusp hits where" with the fence post
  • Working, non-working and protrusive contacts; canine guidance, group function, mutually protected occlusion
  • The five determinants and what makes posterior cusps taller or shorter
  • VDO, VDR, freeway space; the envelope of motion in three planes; postural vs clinical rest position; Bennett movement; articulator parts

Dr. Givan opened the course by revisiting last spring's introduction, because "this is fundamental. This is sort of the starting point." The review has three parts: static and dynamic occlusion, mandibular motion, and articulators. He also pointed to a help sheet in Canvas, "Help! What cusp hits where?", because questions on which cusp contacts where come up "repeatedly through the years" on exams and boards.

Speaking the same language

Occlusion is the static relationship between the incising or masticating surfaces of the maxillary and mandibular teeth (or tooth analogs). Articulation is the static and dynamic contact relationship during function. People use them interchangeably, "but they're not quite the same."

The neutral zone is the potential space between the lips and cheeks on one side and the tongue on the other, where their forces are equal. It is thought to guide where teeth develop. Restored or orthodontically moved teeth should be within it: put something in the way of those muscles "and they'll just sort of knock it out of the way." An imbalance shows up developmentally, for example as an anterior open bite.

The occlusal plane (older term: plane of occlusion) is the average plane established by the incisal and occlusal surfaces. It is not really flat; it is the planar mean of their curvature, and it is one of the keys to good outcomes when rebuilding a patient.

CurvePlane seen inDefinition
Curve of SpeeSagittal (median)From the mandibular canine cusp tip along the buccal cusp tips of the premolars and molars, through the anterior border of the ramus, to the anterior-most part of the condyle (Graf von Spee, 1890)
Curve of WilsonFrontalMediolateral curve of the cusps in both arches: concave in the mandibular arch, convex in the maxillary. Follows the posterior teeth erupting tipped (maxillary angled out, mandibular angled in)
Compensating curveBothThe anteroposterior and mediolateral curving of artificial teeth, used to develop balanced (denture) occlusion. "Curve of Spee is specific for teeth"
Sphere of MonsonThree-dimensionalEach cusp conforms to an imaginary sphere of about 4-inch radius centered near the glabella

How the arches fit

Opposing cusps ideally meet along the central fossa line. Normally the maxillary lingual cusps sit in the mandibular central fossa line and the mandibular buccal cusps sit in the maxillary central fossa line. Reverse articulation (crossbite) flips it: maxillary buccal and mandibular lingual cusps in the opposing fossae. It comes from a discrepancy in arch size or eruption, and "there is absolutely functionally no problem with this." After bone loss most posterior implant crowns have to be built in crossbite; just design them so they don't trap the cheek.

The maxillary arch is longer and wider than the mandibular, but not by much (average arch length about 128 vs 126 mm, with great variation). Arch length runs from the distal of the last tooth on one side, through the contact areas, to the distal of the last tooth on the other.

Posterior tooth form

The occlusal table, between the buccal and lingual cusp tips, is about 50-60% of the tooth's buccolingual width. Each cusp has a mesial and a distal incline. Proximal contacts sit buccal to the central fossa line, so the lingual embrasures are larger, which returns food toward the tongue. The tongue, cheeks (buccinator) and lips keep replacing food on the table; the tongue works as "a knife, fork, and spoon."

Centric cuspsNon-centric cusps
WhichMaxillary lingual, mandibular buccalMaxillary buccal, mandibular lingual
Other namesSupporting, holding, "stamp" cuspsShearing or guiding cusps
ShapeBroad, rounded, about 1/3 of the B-L widthSharp with definite tips, about 1/6 of the B-L width
JobMaintain the vertical dimension of occlusion; final crushing contactFunctional outer aspect shears food (ideally near-contact, no true contact); minimize cheek and tongue impingement; hold the bolus on the table

MIP, centric occlusion and centric relation

"Terminology is a real problem, especially in occlusion," because our ideas started with dentures. Maximum intercuspation (MIP, MICP, ICP) is the complete intercuspation of the teeth independent of condylar position: a tooth-to-tooth relationship set by muscle engrams to protect the teeth. It is not constant: every restoration, tooth movement or loss changes it, so "I'll just restore to MIP" can get you into trouble. In about 90% of people the joints are not in their stable orthopedic position when the teeth are in MIP.

Centric occlusion (CO) is the tooth contact when the mandible is in centric relation. "Centric" means the joint is centered; "when you hear centric, you immediately turn on, oh, we're talking joint." If Dr. Givan could take one term out of the world with a giant eraser, it would be centric occlusion, because so many people use it to mean MIP. On his exams, centric occlusion always means the contact with the joints seated, never MIP. MIP is neuromuscularly determined; CO is structurally determined.

About 90% of people have a slide between the CO contact and MIP, averaging 1.25 ± 1 mm; a slide that deviates left or right tends to be more problematic. Only about 10% have CO and MIP coincident, which is also where we deliberately rebuild patients who need full reconstruction. The CO contact is often unstable; when we close into it without neuromuscular protection (our muscles seat the joints all the time, especially asleep), we get wear facets, fractures and mobility, which are very common findings.

Centric relation (CR) is the maxillomandibular relationship in which the condyles articulate with the thinnest avascular portion of their discs, the complex in the anterior-superior position against the slopes of the articular eminences. It is independent of tooth contact, clinically discernable when the mandible is directed superiorly and anteriorly (bimanual manipulation, or a leaf gauge or Lucia jig), and restricted to pure rotation about the transverse horizontal axis. His short version: "it's where the condyle is seated in the joint. That's it." Our teeth touch only about 18 minutes a day; the rest of the time the muscles seat the condyles.

MIPCentric occlusion (CO)Centric relation (CR)
What it isTeeth maximally intercuspatedTeeth touching with the joints seatedJoints seated (a joint position)
Depends onTeeth; neuromuscular feedbackThe seated jointJoint anatomy, not teeth
Stable over time?No: changes with every change in the occlusionYes (the joint), but the tooth contact is often unstableYes: reproducible starting point
Key numberDiffer in about 90% of people; slide 1.25 ± 1 mmPure rotation up to about 20-25 mm

Angle classification

ClassMolar relationshipShareNotes
Class I (neutroclusion)Normal interdigitationAbout 70%"Class I malocclusion" = normal molars but crowding or rotations elsewhere
Class II (distoclusion)Mandibular first molar distal to the maxillary first molarAbout 25%Division 1: narrow arch, protruding incisors. Division 2: square arch, retruded centrals, flared laterals, deep overlap (hard to restore)
Class III (mesioclusion)Mandibular first molar mesial to the maxillary first molarAbout 5%Incisors usually edge to edge or in anterior crossbite
Class IV (retired)Distal on one side, mesial on the other-Now each side is classified separately

You can classify at the canines or the first molars. Exam rule: if a question doesn't name the class, assume Class I (after checking it isn't implied indirectly).

Two contact variations: cusp-marginal ridge (the mandibular second premolar buccal cusp and the mandibular molar mesiobuccal cusps land in the opposing embrasures; one tooth against two; most adults; Payne's waxing technique) and cusp-fossa (centric cusps in the opposing fossae; tooth to tooth; considered ideal but rarely natural; follows ideal Spee and Wilson curves; tripodized; P.K. Thomas's technique). Dr. Givan often builds cusp-marginal ridge on purpose, because multiple contacts help prevent supereruption.

What cusp hits where: the fence post

From the help sheet: unless told otherwise, assume Class I and an idealized cusp-fossa occlusion. Draw two rows of fence posts: canine, first premolar, second premolar, then the mesial and distal halves of the first and second molars, for each arch. In Class I each mandibular post sits a half step mesial to its maxillary partner (the mandibular canine slightly in front of the maxillary canine); Class II steps the mandible back one post; Class III brings it forward one tooth. "The only thing you really have to remember on fence posts is how to draw fence posts and what their canine relationships are."

The fence post tells you which opposing cusp comes closest; it is not anatomical, and although the posts look like cusp-marginal ridge, exam questions are usually cusp-fossa. Then use your anatomy:

  • Premolars, Class I and Class III: contacts in the mesial fossae of the maxillary premolars and the distal fossae of the mandibular premolars. Class II is the opposite. So in Class I the buccal cusp of #29 is in the mesial fossa of #4, and the lingual cusp of #5 is in the distal fossa of #28.
  • Molars have an anterior and a posterior opposing contact. The maxillary first molar's posterior contact (from the DB cusp of #30) is highly variable, from the oblique ridge to the distal fossa. The mesiolingual cusp of #3 sits in the central fossa of #30.
  • Anchor and step: to decide whether the MB cusp of #31 hits the mesial fossa of #2 or the distal fossa of #3, start at the first molar's posterior contact (DB of #30) and step back: it must be the mesial fossa of #2.

Anterior relationships and anterior guidance

Growth gives deep overbite, edge-to-edge, or an anterior open bite, properly an "anterior open occlusal relationship": no anterior contact in any occluding position of the posterior teeth ("a bite is a verb"). Vertical overlap (lay term overbite) of 3-5 mm is normal, 3 mm the most accepted; orthodontists often accept 1 mm to make room for lower brackets. Horizontal overlap is the lay "overjet." Together they set anterior guidance: the influence of the contacting anterior surfaces on mandibular movement, determined mostly by the lingual (palatal) morphology of the maxillary incisors.

The joint, briefly

The mandible has a body, angle, ramus, coronoid process and condyle. The temporomandibular joint is the articulation between the temporal bone and the condyle: a diarthrodial, bilateral ginglymus joint that both hinges and slides, with an avascular connective tissue disc between condyle and fossa. "I personally think, because I'm a dentist, that it's the most complicated, most difficult joint in the body."

Eccentric movements and contacts

Any movement away from the intercuspal (or seated) position is eccentric. Protrusive: the mandible moves forward and the condyle comes down the articular eminence, carrying the disc; posterior teeth that fail to separate contact on the distal inclines of the maxillary and mesial inclines of the mandibular teeth. Christensen's phenomenon is the space that opens between the posterior teeth in protrusion as the condyle drops down the eminence; Christensen is remembered for showing that a protrusive record captures the eminence angle. Retrusive: slightly back (posterior temporalis).

In a lateral movement the working (laterotrusive) side is the side the mandible moves toward; its condyle mostly rotates. The non-working side (mediotrusive, "balancing," a denture term) is the other one; its condyle orbits: forward, down and medially along the eminence. Working-side contacts are on the side of the movement; non-working contacts are considered interferences.

Help sheet method for interferences: draw the molars in MIP, then move the mandibular tooth in your mind's eye. For the right molars in a left working movement (right side non-working), a contact can occur between the facial incline of the maxillary palatal cusp and the lingual incline of the mandibular buccal cusp. In a right working movement, the lingual incline of the maxillary palatal cusp meets the buccal incline of the mandibular lingual cusp, and the facial incline of the mandibular buccal cusp meets the lingual incline of the maxillary buccal cusp (an interference if unwanted, group function if wanted). For protrusion draw a sagittal view; for crossbite move the mandibular molar to the buccal and reconsider.

Cusp pathways: on a maxillary tooth you watch a mandibular cusp, so protrusive runs mesial, working runs buccal, non-working runs mesiopalatal. On a mandibular tooth you watch a maxillary cusp and everything reverses: protrusive runs distal, working lingual, non-working distobuccal. In a picture the MIP contact is at the base of the arrow: identify the movement first, eliminate choices, then identify the cusp.

Guidance and the goals of ideal occlusion

Canine guidance (canine-protected articulation): the vertical and horizontal overlap of the canines disengages the posterior teeth in excursions; canines have the buttressing bone and proprioception for it. Group function: several teeth share the working-side contacts (e.g. #7-6-5), useful when the canine has compromised periodontal support, is missing, or is an implant (no proprioception). Today group function means a few anterior teeth and perhaps the first premolar, not every tooth. Which has more influence on posterior separation, anterior or condylar guidance? The closer determinant has the greater impact: anterior guidance, when the patient has it.

The list "you will see over and over": equal, simultaneous, stable centric contacts; occlusal force directed down the long axes; elimination of balancing contacts; canine disclusion or group function of the anterior (and occasionally posterior) teeth. Together that is mutually protected articulation: the posterior teeth protect the anterior teeth from excess force in MIP, and the anterior teeth disengage the posterior teeth in all excursions. Balanced occlusion is for dentures, not natural teeth.

The determinants of posterior morphology

Thielmann's formula: balanced occlusion = (condylar guidance × anterior guidance) / (cusp height × compensating curvature × plane of occlusion). Change one factor and the others must change. For natural teeth, the factors tell you how tall the posterior cusps can be:

FactorConditionPosterior cusps
Condylar guidanceSteeperTaller
Anterior guidanceMore vertical overlapTaller
Anterior guidanceMore horizontal overlapShorter
Plane of occlusionMore parallel to the condylar guidanceShorter
Curve of SpeeMore acuteShorter (the most posterior cusps)
Bennett movementGreater, more superior, or greater immediate side shiftShorter

Horizontal factors set the direction of ridges and grooves (the cusps must "escape" each other). A greater distance from the rotating condyle, a greater distance from the midsagittal plane, and a greater Bennett movement all increase the angle between a cusp's laterotrusive and mediotrusive paths; a greater intercondylar distance decreases it. That is why an articulator much smaller than the patient produces crowns you must adjust.

Vertical dimension

Vertical dimension of occlusion (VDO): the distance between two points with the teeth in contact; supports facial height. Vertical dimension at rest (VDR): the same measure at physiologic rest. Freeway space (interocclusal rest space) = VDR minus VDO, usually 2-6 mm; neither 2 nor 6 is "better." Posterior overclosure (old term posterior bite collapse): loss of occluding vertical dimension as posterior teeth are lost or drift, causing interferences and unhealthy loading; treatment starts by correcting the plane of occlusion.

Mandibular movement and the envelope of motion

Start from CR. Rotation (hinge movement) with the condyles seated opens the incisors about 20-25 mm. Beyond that the condyles must translate down and forward; rotation plus translation reaches about 40-60 mm. Border movements are the limits: the superior contact border is dictated by the teeth; the anterior and posterior opening borders by ligaments and joint anatomy. Posselt's envelope of motion (about 1958) combines the borders in the sagittal, horizontal and frontal planes.

Sagittal view, tracing the lower incisor: from CR, pure rotation down to about 20-25 mm, then rotation plus translation to maximum opening (the posterior opening border). From maximum opening, closing with the jaw fully protruded traces the anterior opening border up to maximum protrusion. The superior contact border runs from the CO contact up and forward into MICP (if they differ), down the anterior guidance to edge-to-edge, flat forward past the incisal edges, then on to maximum protrusion. If CO equals MICP, the border runs straight from CR into the anterior guidance.

Horizontal view (from above): left lateral, left lateral with protrusion, right lateral with protrusion, right lateral. Frontal view: left lateral superior, left lateral opening, right lateral opening, right lateral superior, with the postural position (PP) just below the top. Expect to identify these.

We rarely function at a border, except the superior one. Function happens in a small teardrop below MICP, and most functional activities begin or end at MICP. The postural position is about 2-4 mm below MICP, held by a myotactic reflex against gravity so the teeth can be brought into function immediately. It is often wrongly called the clinical rest position, which is the position of least EMG activity, about 8 mm inferior and 3 mm anterior. Head posture changes the path of closure: in the "alert feeding position" the face is about 30° down, and contacts recorded supine can shift anteriorly when the patient sits up. Dr. Givan checks every restoration upright; about 20% of patients feel a difference.

Mandibular lateral translation (Bennett movement, side shift and many other names) is the mediolateral shift of the mandible toward the working side. It may be immediate (a jump, measured in millimeters) or progressive (measured as an angle, the Bennett angle). It comes with joint laxity and its importance "is still somewhat controversial."

Articulators 101

An articulator is a mechanical instrument representing the TMJs and jaws, to which casts are attached to simulate some or all mandibular movements. It is only really useful when it represents the patient; one much smaller than the patient moves differently, "convenient for a laboratory, but very inconvenient for the people who had to put it inside the patient's mouth." Parts of the Whip Mix 2240 (semi-adjustable): upper and lower members, anterior guide pin (not "incisal pin": "rude to the canines"), anterior guide table, mounting plates, condylar elements (with an articulating fossa) and the centric latch, which holds the instrument on its transverse horizontal hinge axis.

"In occlusion, we're talking in the language of microns." You can feel a 25 µm hair between your teeth; "you have to be a micron dentist."
full.anatomy:
What's tested
  • Ginglymoarthrodial joint; "one bone, two joints"; rotation in the lower compartment, translation in the upper
  • The disc (intermediate zone, borders, medial thickness, not a meniscus) and the retrodiscal tissues
  • Ligaments and what each one limits (capsular, discal, stylomandibular, sphenomandibular, TM inner and outer)
  • Each muscle of mastication: roughly where it attaches, its form and its job; the two bellies of the masseter and of the lateral pterygoid
  • The exam slide of muscles for each mandibular movement (Dr. Givan: the answer "will come from this slide")
  • Suprahyoid vs infrahyoid groups and the floating hyoid

This lecture looks at anatomy "from a clinician's point of view": less about every fossa and ridge, more about how the parts work. Dr. Givan said he presented it at the level he would test; he does not plan to ask about innervation or blood supply, which you covered in gross anatomy.

A complex joint

Dogs and alligators hinge and tear; cows and camels grind with large side-to-side motion; we are in between. A ginglymus joint moves in one plane like a hinge (elbow, knee, finger joints). An arthrodial joint glides between flat surfaces (wrist, ankle, spine). The TMJ does both: a ginglymoarthrodial joint. And it is one bone with two joints: no movement of one side happens without the other, so neither TMJ moves independently. Opening starts as pure rotation about the transverse horizontal axis, then adds translation.

The articular disc

The disc is dense fibrous connective tissue that functions like a bone, which makes the TMJ a compound joint. From the side it is biconcave: a thick anterior border, a thinner intermediate zone, and an even thicker posterior border. The condyle normally sits in the intermediate zone, which is completely avascular with no nerves. From the front, the disc is slightly thicker medially than laterally, so if it slips off the condyle it tends to go forward or medially. The heights of contour of the condyle are the medial and lateral poles. It is improper to call the disc a meniscus, which is crescent-shaped (convex and concave sides), as in the knee.

The disc is attached front and back, dividing the joint into an upper (superior) compartment, disc to temporal bone, where translation happens, and a lower (inferior) compartment, disc to condyle, where rotation happens. So the disc stays over the condyle wherever it goes, always there to cushion. Behind it are the retrodiscal tissues, loaded with vessels and nerves; functioning on them causes substantial pain. Of the two retrodiscal laminae, the superior is elastic and the inferior is collagenous. In front, the superior head of the lateral pterygoid attaches to the capsule and disc and the inferior head to the condylar neck. The articulating surfaces are covered by resilient, collagenous, fluid-filled tissue; they are not meant to touch each other, and when a perforated disc lets bone meet bone, the joint breaks down.

The joint is load-bearing. To crush a bolus you need something to pivot against, and that is the seated joint, which is why the condyles seat essentially every time the elevator muscles contract. The condyle's trabecular structure is built like a bridge to carry that force.

Ligaments limit motion

LigamentWhereLimits / does
CapsularCondylar neck to the articular eminence and fossa, wrapping the joint like a curtainEncases the joint; resists downward displacement
Medial and lateral discal (collateral)Disc to the medial and lateral poles of the condyleKeep the disc on the condyle; stretched or torn = clicking (about half of a class clicks)
StylomandibularStyloid process to the angle and posterior border of the ramusLimits opening and forward motion
SphenomandibularSpine of the sphenoid to the lingula of the mandibular foramenLimits opening and forward motion
TM ligament, outer oblique portionSling around the posterior condylar neck to the articular eminenceLimits rotational opening
TM ligament, inner horizontal portionArticular eminence to the disc and condylar headLimits posterior movement of the condyle and disc (protects against a blow to the chin)

Ligaments don't heal, so stretched discal ligaments require other adaptations. If a patient can't close after a long appointment, the condyle may be stuck in front of the eminence (an open lock). Apply gentle downward pressure on the buccal shelf to distract it, "not a posterior force."

How muscles work

Muscles only pull, like a rope. They work as agonist-antagonist pairs, and the opposing muscle never fully turns off, which gives smooth movement at the right speed and force. Muscle fibers are grouped into units that can be activated separately, so one muscle can produce several movements (e.g. the temporalis elevates, protrudes or retrudes). Design depends on the surface available for attachment, speed of contraction, range of movement and force of contraction. Look at a muscle's shape and orientation and you can predict what it does.

The muscles of mastication (supramandibular)

MuscleFormOrigin → insertionJob
MasseterFlat, thick, quadrangular; most superficialZygomatic arch and malar process → angle of the ramus (and coronoid process)Power closer. Superficial belly: elevation + some protrusion. Deep belly: elevation + retrusion. About 50° between the bellies
TemporalisFlat, fan-shaped, bipennateTemporal fossa and fascia → coronoid processPositioner, not a power closer. Anterior: elevation; middle: elevation + some retrusion; posterior: retrusion + some elevation
Lateral pterygoidTriangular, two headsSuperior head: infralateral greater wing of the sphenoid and infratemporal crest → capsule and disc. Inferior head: lateral surface of the lateral pterygoid plate → pterygoid fovea of the condylar neckInferior head: opening and protrusion; one side alone = movement to the opposite side. Superior head: active in closure, stabilizing the disc
Medial pterygoidRhomboidalMedial surface of the lateral pterygoid plate (plus palatine process and maxillary tuberosity) → inferoposterior medial surface of the ramusElevation; with the masseter forms the pterygomasseteric sling

The masseter is not vertical: its fibers run up and forward, so contracting it pushes the mandible superiorly and anteriorly, which is exactly the seated (CR) position. When the jaw is wide open the big superficial belly is folded back without mechanical advantage, so the deep belly starts the closure and swings the superficial belly into position to crush.

The temporalis inserts on the thin coronoid process: "your first thought should be, that's not a power position." It is the jaw's major, fast positioner, aligning the teeth for chewing and shaping the cavity for speech, and its posterior fibers pull the mandible back. It is so important that the zygomatic arch forms a tunnel to protect its insertion.

The lateral pterygoid is really two muscles ("could I just rename these muscles?"). The inferior head pulls the condyle forward, down and toward the midline: both sides = protrusion and opening; one side = the chin swings to the other side ("if I contract on the right side, I will move my jaw to the left"). The superior head is relaxed during opening and active during closure, balancing the elastic pull of the superior retrodiscal lamina so the disc returns smoothly, and keeping the disc in place when you pivot on a bolus. The medial pterygoid is "the unsung hero": a meaty elevator on the inside of the ramus that, with the masseter outside, forms the powerful pterygomasseteric sling.

The exam slide: muscles for each movement

"If I ask a question regarding what muscle is involved in what motion, it will come from this slide," even though other sources list more contributors. And know which belly: "this slide does not signify which belly of the lateral pterygoid, I expect you to know this as well."

MovementMuscles (exam slide)
ElevationTemporalis, medial pterygoid, masseter
DepressionLateral pterygoid (inferior head) + suprahyoid and infrahyoid muscles
ProtrusionLateral pterygoid (inferior head) + superficial masseter
RetrusionTemporalis (horizontal, posterior fibers) + deep masseter
Lateral to the rightRight temporalis + right masseter; left lateral pterygoid + left medial pterygoid
Lateral to the leftLeft temporalis + left masseter; right lateral pterygoid + right medial pterygoid

Opening: the inframandibular muscles and the hyoid

The antagonists of the closers lie below the mandible, divided by the hyoid bone, "one of the coolest bones in the body": it articulates with nothing and floats, and every horn and fossa is a muscle attachment. The suprahyoid (inframandibular) muscles, digastric, geniohyoid, mylohyoid and stylohyoid, help open the jaw. The infrahyoid muscles, sternohyoid, omohyoid, sternothyroid and thyrohyoid, stabilize the hyoid. To open, the infrahyoids first fix the hyoid "like a rock," then the suprahyoids pull the mandible down. The digastric has anterior and posterior bellies joined by an intermediate tendon on the hyoid and is a key opener; the mylohyoid forms the floor of the mouth; the geniohyoid matters for the tongue. To swallow, the teeth come together to stabilize the mandible and the hyoid is pulled forward to open the esophageal path. The superficial neck muscles (sternocleidomastoid and trapezius) act as a sling that maintains head position.

Take-homes: the orientation, size and shape of a muscle tell you what it does, and the bones show how much force the system handles.
full.function:
What's tested
  • Primary vs secondary functions; muscles and ligaments position the jaw when the teeth are apart
  • Neural control: central pattern generator, engrams, reflexes
  • The chewing cycle: phases, 16-18 mm open and 5-6 mm lateral, return to ICP, tooth contact patterns
  • Chewing differences: food hardness, cusp form, TMJ pain, one-sided chewing; bite force numbers and where force is highest
  • Swallowing: what triggers it, somatic vs visceral, force and counts, the three stages
  • Speech: no tooth contact; fricatives (f, v) and the wet-dry line; "s" and closest speaking space

When we move our jaws we have limits (the border movements), but we rarely go there except the superior border. Most function happens with the teeth apart and far from the borders, which keeps it fast. "When the teeth are not in contact, mandibular position is determined by the muscles and ligaments (not anterior or condylar guidance)." Teeth only influence motion when they touch.

The masticatory (stomatognathic) system has three primary functions, mastication, swallowing (deglutition) and speech, and two secondary ones, respiration and expression of emotions.

Part 1: mastication

The masticatory cycle is the rhythmic, well-controlled separation and closure of the teeth; all the movement is the mandible's (if your maxilla moves, "you need a surgeon"). It is the first step of digestion, so the body prioritizes it. The CNS receives afferent input from the PDL, tongue, TMJs, periosteum, muscle spindles and mucosa; the brainstem and up to the thalamus process it quickly (pleasure keeps us eating; a filled stomach inhibits it), and efferents activate some muscle groups and inhibit others. Noxious stimuli are avoided by reflexes: biting a hard surprise triggers a polysynaptic reflex that stops the closers and fires the openers at once, while a simpler myotactic reflex maintains posture.

A central pattern generator times activity between antagonistic muscles and creates learned patterns called engrams. It is mostly subconscious but can be brought under conscious control, like breathing or walking, and it constantly adjusts the stroke from feedback such as particle size. Much of this came from chewing studies (Case Western's Gnathic Replicator, then the University of Florida) that are reproduced today with jaw tracking like ModJaw.

The chewing stroke has an opening phase (more vertical, with a lateral slide at the end) and a closing component: the crushing phase (gradual vertical and horizontal motion that traps the bolus, closing at an angle because the posterior teeth are inclined) and then the grinding phase (a small lateral slide at the very end). Chewing opens only about 16-18 mm and moves about 5-6 mm laterally.

Seen from the side on the working (food) side, the mandible opens anteriorly, then moves posteriorly in early closure, aligning the teeth with the masseter's maximum force vector. On the non-working side movement is mostly vertical, and its condyle moves more and stays anteriorly positioned during closure (the slides add that the working-side condyle is often posterior to CR during closure). Early chewing has more anterior movement (incising) and more lateral movement; both decrease as the food breaks down. Harder food means more lateral movement and more power; some patients don't change their stroke count with texture.

About 78% of patients chew mostly on one side, usually the side with the most contacts in lateral glide. That loads the TMJs unequally, normally without problems because the superior lateral pterygoids stabilize the discs.

Early studies predicted no tooth contact during chewing, but some does occur, and contacts return to ICP every time: "no matter how you run around the bases, you always come back to home plate." Contact increases as the bolus breaks down, to nearly every stroke before the swallow. The average contact lasts about 194 ms. Gliding contacts (cusp inclines passing each other) occur in the opening (56%) and grinding (60%) phases; single contacts occur close to MICP.

Cusp form shapes the stroke: tall cusps and deep fossae promote a mostly vertical stroke; flattened cusps encourage a broader, more horizontal one. In a heavy bruxer, MIP "becomes a range... a zone," because they can close almost anywhere. Patients with TMJ pain chew with less repeatable, slower, shorter and more irregular strokes.

Bite forceValue
Greatest ever measured975 lb-force
Male maximum118-142 lb
Female maximum79-99 lb
First molar91-198 lb
Incisor29-51 lb
Carrots / meatAbout 30 lb / about 16 lb
DenturesAbout 25% of maximum (Dr. Givan: closer to 15%)

Force drops the farther you are from the condyles: the first molar has about three to five times the force of the central incisor, which is how anterior teeth get away with off-axis loading. Bite force rises with age to maturity and with practice (tough diets); men are higher than women, though body size matters more. A high FMA (divergent jaws, long face) means lower forces; a square, low-angle face means high forces. With unilateral chewing of bread, forces on both sides are about equal. A restoration left 0.5 mm high doubles the force. With tougher foods, chewing happens mostly at the second premolar and first molar, which supports the shortened dental arch concept. Anterior slides of the teeth (a "long centric") are rarely seen in function.

The tongue handles taste and sensation, divides the food, puts it back on the chewing surfaces, forms the bolus and sweeps the teeth after the swallow, "our knife, fork, and spoon." It couldn't do it without the buccinator, which forms a controlled wall and returns food from the vestibule.

Part 2: swallowing

Deglutition is a series of muscle contractions that moves a bolus from the mouth through the esophagus to the stomach, partly voluntary but mostly involuntary and reflex. (Gustation = tasting; olfaction = smelling; anosmic = complete loss of smell; hyposmic = reduced smell.) The not-necessarily-conscious decision to swallow depends on the fineness of the food, the intensity of taste extracted, and the lubrication of the bolus.

Stabilizing the mandible is what matters most, so the hyoid can move. Adults use a somatic swallow: the teeth come together in MIP and the elevators hold the mandible there. A visceral (infantile) swallow braces the mandible by pushing the tongue forward between the arches; it is normal until the posterior teeth erupt (and when swallowing liquids), but if over-retained it displaces teeth anteriorly, e.g. an anterior open bite. Swallowing contacts are heavy and long, about 66.5 lb for about 683 ms, 7.8 lb more than chewing, and they happen in ICP, not a retruded position as once thought. We swallow about 590 times a day: 146 during meals, 394 between meals while awake (mostly saliva) and 50 asleep.

StageWhat happensTime
1 (voluntary)The tongue separates the food; the bolus on its dorsum is pressed lightly against the palate, tongue tip behind the incisors; lips sealed, teeth closed; a reflex wave pushes the bolus back into the pharynxStages 1 + 2 about 1 second
2Pharyngeal constrictor peristalsis carries the bolus to the esophagus; the soft palate rises and seals the nasal passage; the epiglottis closes over the trachea; the Eustachian tube openings open (normally closed)
3Peristalsis carries the bolus to the cardiac sphincter, which relaxes into the stomach; the upper esophagus has some voluntary control to return food for more chewing6-7 seconds

Swallowing is studied by videofluoroscopic swallowing study, dynamic MRI and (historically) cinefluorography. For patients who can't wear dentures but struggle to swallow, a record-base-like appliance gives them something to stabilize against.

Part 3: speech

The diaphragm forces air from the lungs; controlled contraction and relaxation of the vocal cords sets pitch (B vs P, D vs T, G vs K differ only by voicing). The tongue, lips, cheeks and mandible shape the cavity for resonance and articulation. Most speech uses a prolonged expiration with a quick breath at a pause. After learning, speech is totally subconscious, a "learned reflex." Tooth contacts do not normally occur in speech: it is too rapid, and contact would damage teeth. Malpositioned teeth can still affect the sound.

  • Fricatives (f, v): the maxillary incisal edge should lightly touch the wet-dry line (vermilion border) of the lower lip. Can't make the sound: incisors may be too short. Depressing the lip: too long. Clinically important when placing incisors a patient no longer has.
  • Sibilants (s): the teeth come closest, about 1-1.5 mm apart. "Let S be your guide": the closest speaking space helps set a functional vertical dimension.
  • M: nasopharynx open, tongue neutral, teeth apart, lips together. P and B: plosives, lips together, soft palate sealed. K and G: back of the tongue against the soft palate, anterior teeth slightly apart.
  • T and D: tongue against the palate behind the teeth, so the cingulum contour matters. Wide-open vowels and diphthongs ("eight," "nine") separate the teeth about 5-10 mm.

"In chewing and swallowing, I am amazed by the orchestration of so many different muscle groups... occurring without conscious thought, rapidly, repeatedly, and with great efficiency."
full.concepts:
What's tested
  • Who contributed what: Bonwill, Balkwill, von Spee, Bennett, Christensen, Monson, Pankey-Mann-Schuyler, the gnathologists (Stallard and Stuart, D'Amico, P.K. Thomas)
  • PMS vs gnathology: what each assumed, which instruments, what they learned
  • The modern ideas (conformative, gnathology, Pankey/Dawson, bioesthetics, neuromuscular): what they share and how they differ
  • The four modern concepts: posterior support (first), plane of occlusion, occlusal contacts (tripodization vs point to surface, freedom), anterior guidance
  • Shortened dental arch; the custom anterior guide table; Dawson's smile design steps and phonetics

Patients rarely look like the ideal dentoform, but "do principles of normal occlusion apply? Yes." The fundamentals came from about 175 years of ideas, first for dentures, then (about a century later) applied to natural teeth, where some didn't work.

Where the ideas came from

WhoWhenContribution
W.G.A. Bonwill, "father of articulation"ca. 1858Equilateral triangle: about 4 inches (110 mm) condyle to condyle to the mandibular symphysis (from thousands of skulls). Led to the occlusal plane concept and the first scientifically based arrangement: bilaterally balanced occlusion. Articulators still use 110 mm intercondylar widths
F.H. Balkwill1866The translating condyle moves medially in lateral movement, 40 years before Bennett
Count von Spee1890The occlusal curve in the sagittal plane
I.M. Bromill1897Diagrammed facial planes; anatomic landmarks for tooth positions
Carl Christensen1901Arc of mandibular movement; posterior separation in protrusion; the protrusive record
J.B. Parfitt1902First to put curved condylar paths on an articulator
Norman G. Bennett1908Lateral translation of the mandible
George Monsonca. 1916Spherical theory: combined the 4-inch triangle, bilateral balance, Spee's curve and Balkwill's and Christensen's condylar observations into a 4-inch sphere. His instrument did not reproduce the condyles; it used a central rotational center with set screws

In the 1800s, a geometric relationship was thought to mean something about function. The 4-inch triangle is real (it still holds on CT scans), but it doesn't dictate how we should function. Still, dentures built on Monson's sphere were generally very successful, and curve-following setups are still used, especially when many teeth are missing.

Two schools, 1930s to 1970s

Pankey, Mann and Schuyler (PMS) combined Monson's theory with Meyer's functionally generated path (FGP, 1933): the mandibular posteriors were restored to the 4-inch sphere, then the maxillary posteriors were built from an FGP, pathways the patient ground into wax. They argued an instrument reproducing condylar motion was unnecessary because the FGP recorded it, and used a simple suspension articulator with a big base. Applying denture balance to teeth didn't work, so Schuyler evolved the concept: eliminate balancing contacts, elevate anterior guidance, use contact areas rather than point contacts, and adopt simpler instruments (the Hanau H2 semi-adjustable articulator, an arbitrary face-bow and the Broadrick occlusal plane analyzer, a "flag" scribed with a 4-inch arc from the canine and distal molar).

Gnathology (from McCollum's work) aimed to replicate the patient exactly: locate the rotational centers of the condyles in all three dimensions, record every border movement with a pantograph, and program a fully adjustable articulator, so restorations made on it would need little adjustment. Early goals: MICP coincident with CR in the rearmost, uppermost, midmost (RUM) position (wrong by today's understanding: "you need a good glass of rum"), and bilateral balance in excursions ("Yikes!"). The gnathologists then contributed lasting ideas: Stallard and Stuart, cuspid protection (canine guidance), keyword disclusion; D'Amico, mutually protected occlusion, keyword force (anterior teeth handle off-axis forces better); Peter K. Thomas, cusp-fossa waxing (your PKT instruments); Niles Guichet, simpler (but still complex) fully adjustable instruments. Gnathology "could rarely be achieved," and its followers blamed the instruments, not the philosophy. Digital jaw tracking (e.g. ModJaw feeding a virtual articulator) has revived its goal of representing the patient.

Modern concepts combine both schools, and by the mid-1990s they were pretty well defined.

Differing modern ideas

IdeaCore
ConformativeMatch what is there; don't change the existing occlusion. About 90-98% of general dentistry, when the patient is healthy and asymptomatic
GnathologyCapture the condyles' axes in 3-D; posterior occlusal anatomy should replicate condylar motion
Pankey / DawsonFrom PMS; respects CR (when to use it to diagnose and treat) and elevates anterior guidance as the major controlling factor
BioestheticsForm, function and esthetics are linked; VDO can be set arbitrarily from a fixed interarch measurement; strong anterior vertical overlap allows more esthetic posterior cusps
NeuromuscularJankelson; the LVI. Restore at the "myocentric point" of least muscle activity found with a TENS unit (Myo-Monitor). Requires an increased vertical, i.e. full-mouth rehabilitation, and a more forward position without joint stability; not taught at UAB

All have some success, because patients adapt. They agree that all teeth should touch at once and that back teeth shouldn't interfere when the jaw moves. They differ on the maxillomandibular (condylar) relationship, the VDO, and the envelope of function and anterior guidance. Frank Speer: "What a patient does to an occlusion may be more important than the occlusion itself." He asked two questions of any philosophy: can you apply it to all patients, and can you apply it without having to restore teeth?

The goals of modern occlusion are the same list as Lec1: stable centric contacts, force down the long axes, no balancing contacts, canine disclusion or anterior group function: mutually protected occlusion, in MIP or CO, laterally and in protrusion.

Four modern concepts

1. Posterior support ("building the dance floor"). Usually the first consideration in a restorative plan; anterior guidance follows closely as the second. "Support first, disclusion second." Without posterior teeth the anteriors take all the force and chewing work and decline fast, and the jaw overcloses (posterior overclosure, old term posterior bite collapse), leaving less restorative space. Patients often want their "social six" treated; spending their savings on six anterior crowns without posterior support is doomed. How much support? The shortened dental arch: restoring to the second premolar shows no difference in chewing ability, TMD, tooth migration, periodontal support or comfort; the WHO considers at least 20 natural teeth functional and esthetic. Esthetics may suffer where first molars show.

2. Plane of occlusion. Supraeruption, tilting and rotation, interferences and malocclusion prevent an ideal plane, and a violated plane makes disclusion impossible. Dr. Givan's regretted early case: crowns placed against an extruded opposing molar that interfered in every excursion. Fix the plane first: enameloplasty for about half a millimeter, a crown to shorten more, and sometimes extraction when intentional endo plus crown lengthening (into the furcation) is too much.

3. Occlusal contacts. Replicating occlusal anatomy (cusps, ridges, grooves) matters, matched to the patient (flatter crowns for a flat-cusped bruxer). Tripodization (from gnathology): each cusp tip contacts the opposing fossa on three surfaces, up to 27 contacts across a quadrant; excellent stability, difficult in metal and extremely difficult in porcelain, no wiggle room so it requires immediate disclusion; suggested only when the opposing surfaces are controlled or in full reconstruction. Point to surface (modern): a cusp tip contacts a flat surface, so force goes down the long axis and there is horizontal freedom, especially valuable with an immediate lateral translation; used regardless of the extent of treatment. Move contacts off inclines and give room before anterior disclusion: "freedom in the functional area." Mediolateral freedom lets the immediate lateral translation happen without an interference; anteroposterior freedom allows the slide from the CR contact to MICP, a long centric.

4. Anterior guidance. The most important determinant and the one you control most, through the lingual contours of the maxillary anterior teeth. They must accommodate the functional opening, closing and eccentric pathways, the envelope of function (contact near the cingulum, a flatter zone, then steeper, following the chewing pattern). Without good anterior guidance (anterior open bite, minimal overlap, edge to edge), you rely on condylar guidance, which is far less effective. Gnathologists focused on posterior guidance; modern philosophy sides with Schuyler that anterior guidance matters more. To build it: diagnostic wax-up → provisionals tried in the mouth → capture their pathways in a custom anterior guide table (or scan them digitally) → final crowns follow the same pathways.

Dawson's 7-step smile design

StepWhat to check
1. Centric stopsHolding contacts on the lingual of the maxillary anteriors; the contours must still disclude the posteriors
2. Lip supportEmergence from the labial gingiva. A gingival bulge is a common lab compensation for an under-prepared tooth; measure the provisionals' thickness
3. Lip closureUnstrained closure; space for guidance; no heavy contact on the lower lip
4. Tooth to lip"F and v should be your friends": incisal edge at the wet-dry line; edges follow the smile line. The provisionals are the real test
5. Lingual contoursVerify CR holding contacts, check need for a long centric, smooth protrusive function, decide single vs group lateral guidance for posterior disclusion
6. Cingulum contourRounded for normal d and t sounds; over-bulked on a tongue-thrust patient = labial tooth movement (but holding contact is vital)
7. Verify with "s"Closest speaking space: too much space = lisp, too little = teeth bump or whistle. Done right, the contours sit within the neutral zone

From very "crazy" ideas (they weren't crazy at the time) to 2026: all teeth touching in centric, posteriors discluded in eccentrics, mutually protected occlusion.
full.applying:
What's tested
  • Accepted schemes; copy the existing guidance when there are no signs or symptoms
  • MIP facts (17.5 minutes a day, 1,800 chewing strokes, 500 swallowing contacts); PDL senses 20 µm
  • What to check in working, non-working and protrusive movements
  • Conformative vs reorganized: when to use each, CR vs MIP records, registration materials and errors
  • Restoration by restoration: intracoronal, single crowns (bounded and end of arch), three-unit, quadrants, Class III and IV composites, anterior crowns, the custom anterior guide table
  • Closest speaking space; natural tooth vs implant movement; anterior vs posterior implant occlusion

"It really comes down to applying occlusion... where the rubber hits the road," mostly in restorative dentistry (based on Dr. Perng-Ru Liu's presentation). Patients rarely fit the textbook: tipped teeth give protrusive interferences, and problems such as wear facets, fractures through crowns and mobility often exist before symptoms do. Replacing a fractured crown doesn't fix the force that broke it.

Schemes and guidance

Accepted occlusal schemes: balanced (dentures; tried on teeth once, "bad idea"), mutually protected, and group function (today a canine, lateral and maybe the first premolar, not every tooth). Group function or canine guidance? In the absence of signs or symptoms, copy the existing guidance when restorations are needed. That is conformative dentistry.

MIP is the complete intercuspation regardless of condylar position, the end of the chewing cycle, where maximum chewing force is applied and the mandible is stabilized to swallow, and it is not stable over the long term. In a day the teeth meet in MIP for only about 17.5 minutes: about 1,800 chewing strokes and 500 swallowing contacts (657,000 chewing strokes a year). Clenching is the pathologic exception. Healthy contacts mean no mobility, no wear, no fractures.

In lateral excursions, check working contacts (canine guidance or group function) for mobility of the guiding teeth (splinting?) and for smooth vs restricted movement; contacts back in the posterior from plane problems, drifting or tooth loss hurt muscle function. A non-working contact tends to guide the mandible during lateral excursion; check mobility on the non-working side and the corresponding working contacts. A patient who has adapted to one over years can keep it, but patients don't tolerate one you introduce in an afternoon; reshape with enameloplasty when needed. The PDL detects material down to about 20 µm. In protrusion, check the direction, mobility, and any posterior contact: posterior protrusive interferences must be eliminated before restoring the anterior teeth. Sometimes anterior contours can give enough separation, but you can't make guidance steep enough to clear a badly tipped molar.

Two approaches

ConformativeReorganized
IdeaRestoration in harmony with the existing jaw relationshipsThe entire occlusal scheme is changed, in harmony with new jaw relationships
Allowed changesLocalized only: shorten an opposing cusp, eliminate non-working interferences, remove a deflective contact on the tooth to be restoredStart "from ground zero" with the joints seated first: a reproducible starting point, an even stable occlusion, no iatrogenic deflective contacts
RecordMIP record: for working casts; as minimal as requiredCR record (bimanual manipulation): also for mounting diagnostic casts
WhenMost general dentistry, if the occlusion is healthy and asymptomaticWhen conforming is unsafe: destruction, wear, fractures, or large multi-quadrant work

How do you know conformative is safe? At diagnosis, compare the contact with the joints seated (CO) with the MIP contact; a big or deviating difference plus wear, fracture, mobility or tooth movement says copying is not enough.

Registration materials: elastomeric PVS (Regisil), thermoplastic waxes (Aluwax), zinc oxide eugenol plaster, acrylics and plaster of Paris. PVS is an excellent impression material but sets in 20-30 seconds while the patient moves; warmed wax chilled with the air-water syringe hardens in 1-2 seconds. Common errors: a full-arch registration (you've put material between teeth that should touch) and untrimmed excess (you can't verify the mounting). A correct MIP record sits only where teeth are not in contact (the preps), is trimmed to the cusp tips and kept off soft tissue, and the contacts you see in the mouth (e.g. #26 on #8) must show on the mounting. With elastomers: constant occlusal pressure while setting, trim with a scalpel before mounting, and press the casts while mounting to avoid rebound. Best of all, hand-articulate when you can: "any material that we use is going to increase error."

Posterior restorations

For any posterior intracoronal restoration you want a stable relationship with the opposing tooth and simultaneous contacts with the other teeth in MIP. You don't want deflective contacts, high spots, infraocclusion (the tooth will supererupt, "and it never supererupts in a good contact"), non-working contacts or working interferences.

  • Single intracoronal: small, fit the existing relationships. Large, check the opposing cusp for over-eruption and non-working contacts and make localized adjustments before placing it.
  • Multiple intracoronal: conformative for multiple small restorations without an over-erupted cusp. Localized modification for an over-erupted cusp into a worn or scooped-out restoration, non-working contacts, plunger cusps (cusps violating the plane of occlusion) and deflective contacts. Reorganized for multiple large restorations in posterior quadrants (use materials with high initial compressive and tensile strength).
  • Single bounded crown: usually conformative; check and adjust the opposing cusp first; registration by hand articulation, PVS or Aluwax; no face-bow; hinge-type articulator (semi-adjustable rarely). At try-in: fully seated, proximal contacts first, then occlusion.
  • Single crown at the end of the arch: the same, except adjust any retruded deflective contact first and use an occlusal registration to mount (the cast easily drops posteriorly).
  • Three-unit bridge (bounded or end of arch): usually conformative (generally fine up to three units in the posterior); ensure the opposing arch has a desirable occlusal plane; PVS or Aluwax; semi-adjustable (arcon) articulator, hinge sometimes OK. A four-unit bridge replaces about half the patient's occlusion, so "what do you put back?"
  • Quadrants: ensure a desirable opposing plane (crown lengthening, opposing crowns, root canal therapy may be needed); more indication for equilibration first. Restoring opposing quadrants lets you build a favorable plane and curve of Spee.

Articulators: "there's never an advantage to the dentist" of a small hinge articulator; the advantage is entirely the laboratory's. One the size of the patient, even a semi-adjustable left at average settings, makes arcs closer to the patient's, so less adjusting at the hardest place to work, beside the tongue.

Anterior restorations

  • Class III composite: copy the existing contacts; avoid centric and protrusive contact on the restorative material.
  • Class IV composite: simultaneous centric and protrusive contact on the natural tooth AND the restoration to reduce fracture and differential wear, especially edge to edge. All the guidance on a Class IV is "a recipe for disaster."
  • Single anterior crown: without symptoms, in harmony with the existing occlusion; correct posterior deflective contacts that slide the mandible forward into the incisors, especially with a history of fracture.
  • Multiple maxillary anterior crowns: need a customized anterior guide table when restoring both central incisors or one or both canines. The guide pin's pathways capture the full functional range of the guidance. To copy the guidance unchanged, make the impression for the guide before preparing the teeth.

Inadequate anterior guidance (missing, malaligned or broken-down anteriors): diagnostic wax-up at a tentative VDO → provisionals from its matrix (guidance and esthetics) → observe for several weeks (at least three if mild and asymptomatic; months for a bruxer) → custom anterior guide table from the corrected provisionals → definitive lingual contours follow the guide. The tentative VDO uses the closest speaking space: about 1-2 mm between the incisal edges while the patient unconsciously repeats "s" (counting 60 to 70). Too much space gives a lisp, too little a whistle.

Implants

An implant is a titanium root locked in bone, with no periodontal ligament, so it moves far less than a tooth:

Under about 10 lbNatural toothDental implant
ApicalAbout 28 µmAbout 2-3 µm (bone microstrain)
Lateral56-75 µm posterior; 90-108 µm anterior10-50 µm

Anterior implants: centric contact very light in casual intercuspation and equal to the neighbors in maximum intercuspation; in excursions avoid immediate canine disclusion and share the load with the natural teeth, which have proprioception. Posterior implants: very light in casual closure, equal in maximum intercuspation (no contact lets the opposing tooth supererupt); avoid contact in excursions if possible; mutually protected occlusion. Test with shimstock (about 12 µm): on a light closure it holds on the neighbors and pulls through the implant with some resistance; on a clench the teeth drop into their PDL and it holds on all of them.

Summary: most of general dentistry is conformative, but look first. Check the opposing plane of occlusion, the contacts, any deflections and the direction of forces; copy what the patient has only if it is asymptomatic and healthy.
full.instruments:
What's tested
  • Why we mount casts: diagnosis (CR vs MIP mountings), treatment planning, diagnostic waxing, treatment
  • Arcon vs non-arcon; the UAB classification (non-adjustable, semi-adjustable, fully adjustable)
  • Non-adjustable articulators: accurate in one position only, who benefits, mounting without a facebow
  • Semi-adjustable: sagittal condylar inclination and the Bennett angle; the facebow, CR record, MIP record and eccentric records, and the errors each one prevents or causes
  • Fully adjustable: kinematic facebow, pantograph, why record thickness doesn't matter there but does on a semi-adjustable
  • Choosing an articulator: the patient's occlusion, the extent of the work, the instrument's limits, the clinician

Dr. Givan opened the second half of the course (10/22) with the devices we use to relate the arches. "It seems every concept of occlusal therapy developed an articulator": many of the old concepts were driven by what a machine could do. Today it is much simpler, and he sorts everything into three groups: you can't adjust it, you can adjust some of it, or you program all of it. The equipment is only a tool; the goal is to treat the patient. His one line to remember: an articulator has its best value when it is similar in size to the patient.

What we use articulators for

Diagnosis. Mounted diagnostic casts improve visualization of the static and functional relationships of the teeth and make it easier to replicate mandibular movement and the contacts it produces. Pathologic contacts often can't be seen clinically, because protective neuromuscular reflexes steer the patient around them, but properly mounted casts show them. A CR mounting is the most useful for diagnosis: it allows the fullest range of movement, so you can evaluate every contact and slide, close into CO (often unstable) and still move into MIP. An MIP mounting can't reposition the condyles to CR, so it can't show the CO contacts. From a CR mounting you can always find MIP; from an MIP mounting you can't get back to CO.

Treatment planning. Mounted casts help build a sequential plan that removes the causes of disease and restores function and esthetics: you can visualize each step on the articulator first, for example a selective grinding (equilibration). Diagnostic waxing develops the tooth forms in wax to see the final goal and the problems that may come up, and to plan spacing, orthodontics, hard and soft tissue grafting, the occlusion, fixed and removable tooth-, implant- and tissue-supported prostheses, and esthetics. It is also used to address the patient's expectations: a patient who doesn't understand dentistry understands a cast in front of them.

Treatment. The most common use of an articulator is treatment: some materials and methods for making a prosthesis aren't appropriate for the mouth (indirect fabrication), and moving the articulator helps build it. "If I could get one point across today": your choice of articulator will make or break your time treating the patient. Anything you can do outside an appointment to make the appointment faster is money well spent; an articulator that replicates the patient makes crown and denture deliveries go much faster.

Classifying articulators

Arcon stands for ARticulating CONdyle: the condylar element is on the lower member of the articulator and the fossa element on the upper member, as in the patient. A non-arcon articulator has them the other way around; it is often cheaper, but, for example, you can't change the vertical dimension as easily without throwing off your records.

The UAB accepted classification has three groups. Non-adjustable: hinge and average-value articulators (not programmable). Semi-adjustable: some settings, some averages (for example the Denar 320, the one you have). Fully adjustable: everything is programmed. Articulators don't fit neatly into these groups: it's a continuum, and some semi-adjustable articulators are nearly fully adjustable.

Virtual articulators in digital dentistry are "not quite yet, but close." Software can replicate a mechanical articulator's shape and motion, and digital work can combine intraoral scans, CBCT data and facial and esthetic landmarks. What they still lack is accurately positioning the models to the patient, the equivalent of a facebow (a digital facebow that puts the maxillary teeth in the same 3-D relation to the joints). Digital is pushing dentistry back toward fully adjustable articulation, which the mechanical world had drifted away from because it was so hard to do.

Non-adjustable articulators

No adjustment can bring a non-adjustable articulator closer to the patient. Its movements range from a hinge only to eccentric movements based on averages. However different they look (a palm-sized hinge, one glued to the back of the cast, one that looks like yours with no adjustments), they are all accurate in only one contact position, MICP. Their opening and closing paths and all their eccentric motions don't reflect the patient.

The procedure is an arbitrary mounting in MICP. Any interocclusal record that separates the teeth increases the error, because when it is removed the articulator closes along a different arc from the patient's mandible. The smaller the articulator compared with the patient, the larger that error.

Advantages: low expense and little effort. But that benefits the lab, not the dentist: labs like these because they are quick, inexpensive and small (low shipping costs), and dentists often don't ask for more ("all you have to do is ask"). Because the articulator doesn't replicate the patient, the restoration can't meet the occlusal requirements of the patient's eccentric movements, so the dentist spends chair time adjusting it, and grinding often destroys anatomic contour and leaves poor occlusal relationships (zirconia, which doesn't adjust or polish well, makes this worse). Partial-arch articulators also can't verify the mounting cross-arch or let you model the occlusal form from the opposite side. "There is never an advantage to the dentist for the lab to use this articulator": its hinge axis can be very different from the anatomic one, sometimes directly behind the second molar, and it can't move in pathways like the patient's. Dentists seem to accept that adjusting crowns is normal: "NO!"

The exception: a non-adjustable articulator about the size of a person, with the condyles roughly 4 inches apart and the maxillary cast placed in about the right orientation to them (for example the Hanau-Mate from Whip Mix), builds crowns that roughly match the patient's movement.

Mounting without a facebow. Use an articulator with an intercondylar distance of about 110 mm (4 inches) and a universal mounting stand. Secure the stand's platform to the lower member; center the maxillary cast on its positioning lines; fix it with utility wax, sticky wax or hot glue; attach it to the upper member's mounting plate with stone or plaster; when that has set, remove the platform; relate the mandibular cast with a bite registration if needed; with the articulator inverted, attach the lower cast to the lower mounting plate; when that has set, turn it upright and remove the registration. The casts are now in the Bonwill position, where the average protrusive angle (condylar inclination), immediate side shift (Bennett movement) and progressive side shift can be used without patient records.

Semi-adjustable articulators

Some settings let a semi-adjustable articulator resemble the patient more closely (how many depends on the model), so occlusal contacts and eccentric motions can be replicated to nearly match the patient. One semi-adjustable articulator can be used for almost anything, from a single crown to a full-mouth reconstruction with a change in vertical dimension, if you know how to use it. Why would you ever restore anterior teeth on a non-adjustable articulator when a semi-adjustable one moves in the right direction? The two common adjustments:

1. Sagittal condylar inclination (SCI), also called condylar guidance: the angle at which the condyle descends the articular eminence in the sagittal plane. It controls the disclusion of the posterior teeth when there is little or no anterior guidance, and it affects cusp height and fossa depth. It can be customized to the patient's eminence (one protrusive record sets both sides) or set arbitrarily: 20-30° is common for fixed work, and about 0° for neutrocentric dentures. Matching the patient's protrusive function is especially helpful for bilateral balanced occlusion in dentures. (Desired touching is a "contact"; undesired touching is an "interference".)

2. Bennett angle: in mediotrusion the orbiting condyle moves inward (anterior, inferior and medial), which affects the width of the central fossae of the posterior teeth. It is the angle of that inward path in the horizontal plane relative to a straight protrusive path, set on the medial wall of the fossa. More sophisticated instruments can also set the immediate lateral mandibular translation (immediate side shift, ISS). The Bennett angle is less commonly adjusted: "if I was going to leave any feature off of an articulator, I'd probably leave this one," because the average values are close enough for most general dentistry.

Because the articulator can be adjusted, information must be gathered from the patient: 1. a facebow transfer (mounts the maxillary cast), 2. a centric relation record and 3. eccentric records (MIP, lateral, protrusive), which mount the mandibular cast and program the articulator. The goal is opening and closing paths as close as possible to the patient's, to minimize interferences.

The facebow transfer

The facebow mounts the maxillary cast (never the mandibular) in a similar relation to the patient's hinge axis, for function and esthetics. It consists of an ear-bow (caliper), a transfer assembly and a bite plate, and it needs a reference plane defined by three points on the patient that are calibrated to the articulator: two posterior points, usually the auditory canals, which estimate the transverse horizontal hinge axis, and one anterior point, which depends on the system (nasion, orbitale, or a set distance from the edge of the maxillary teeth). The reference plane is usually the Frankfort horizontal (some use Camper's plane). In an indirect mounting only the transfer assembly is attached to the lower member of the articulator to mount the cast, which simplifies mounting and lets the ear-bow stay in the clinic.

Facebows for semi-adjustable articulators don't try to locate the exact hinge axis: they estimate an arbitrary posterior point near it, typically within 2-5 mm, much more accurate than a mounting stand. The auditory canals are the clinical reference, but the bow is designed with an arbitrary hinge axis in front of the ears. That is an arbitrary facebow; a bow that locates the exact hinge axis is a kinematic facebow. "99.9% of patients" are treated well with an arbitrary facebow; the small error is clinically insignificant.

The school's clinical guideline for the Denar Slidematic facebow (about 1.5 minutes; in class he said 30-50 seconds): the anterior reference point is 43 mm above the right lateral incisal edge (#7), marked with a ruler (adjacent teeth or the lower border of the upper lip at rest if #7 is missing); PVS on the bite plate captures the cusp tips and incisal edges, held with cotton rolls; the transfer assembly goes on the ear-bow, then into the ear canals; the pointer is aimed at the mark, the bow is checked level (its horizontal level parallels the bench top) and in the facial midline, the clamps are tightened, and the transfer jig goes to the mounting table. The level is what captures the esthetic planes: a cant of the incisal plane and the tilt of the occlusal plane come to the articulator, where you can see them.

Without a facebow the instrument loses much of its value. Incorrect maxillary orientation gives an error in the esthetic plane (risk of an occlusal cant: you hesitate to hand the patient the mirror), an error in the occlusal plane (risk of protrusive, non-working and working interferences), possibly incorrect cusp height, and grooves and cusps that don't match the patient. The result is more chairside adjustment, often ablating anatomic form: more work for the dentist to fix, if possible, what was easily avoided.

Hinge axis and facebow. The facebow relates the maxilla to both the patient's hinge axis (PHA) and the articulator's hinge axis (AHA). With a kinematic facebow, AHA = PHA; with an arbitrary facebow, AHA is near PHA. Mounting errors show up in protrusion and laterotrusion: a cast mounted too posterior or too superior gives premature or heavy contacts on the most anterior teeth; too anterior or too inferior gives premature or heavy contacts on the most posterior teeth.

The centric relation record

CO is often unstable, so an interocclusal record is needed to mount in CR, and from a CR mounting you can easily move to MICP. It is most appropriate for diagnosis, for reorganized dentistry and for changes in VDO. Wax is often preferred: an immediate set (soften it, hit it with the air-water syringe), minimal trimming, repeatable for verification, and because it doesn't capture fine anatomy, the opposing cusp tips seat into it "like clockwork". It is fragile. Some techniques use VPS (the Lucia jig, the leaf gauge).

The record is made without tooth contact, because contact triggers the neuromuscular reflexes that deviate the jaw toward MIP, and at the smallest opening that avoids tooth contact: the more the vertical is opened, the larger the error, because an arbitrary axis is being used. Or make it at the vertical dimension you intend to restore.

Stability of CO. When MIP = CO, the contacts are stable and distributed and the vertical is stable: the ideal mounted relationship for reorganized treatment (dentures, full-mouth rehabilitation, full-arch implant work). But MIP ≠ CO in about 90% of people. Closing with the joints seated, neuromuscular control may not bring the jaw to MIP (sleep, rapid closure), and the resulting interferences lead to wear facets, tooth and cusp fracture, mobility and pain. The closure from CO to MIP decreases the VDO, positions the mandible anteriorly and has many potential interferences. So the CR mounting matters most for diagnosis, while treatment is usually conformative.

The MIP record

Mounting in MIP (also called MICP or ICP) is simpler than a CR mounting, because MICP is often more stable than CO, and it is the most appropriate for conformative restorative dentistry. Its significant limitation: the casts can't move posteriorly-superiorly to show any slide from CO to MICP, and since the start isn't joint-seated, eccentric motion is inaccurate unless it is tooth guided.

It is the most common record and "also the most misused record." The number one cause of lab problems is a bad impression; the second is the mounting, usually from misusing MIP records. The most important rule: hand-articulate the casts whenever you can, and use a registration only if they are unstable. If you send the lab a record, they will mount with it, so don't send one "just in case."

VPS (vinyl polysiloxane, polyvinyl siloxane) is the common material, but it must be trimmed to seat accurately, and its resilience is a problem without adequate posterior stops. Its working time is 30-60 seconds minimum from the start of the mix at 72°F (22°C) and its minimum removal time 1 minute 30 seconds: hard to hold still, and a patient who moves as it sets distorts it invisibly. It is also hard to reseat clinically to confirm the registration. Waxes are generally easier and highly accurate: aluminous wax (Aluwax) or resinous wax (Delar), an instant set with the air-water syringe, little or no trimming, much lower cost; but they need a water bath, are brittle, and can get too thin for an MIP record.

If you use VPS: don't cover the occluding surfaces of unprepared teeth (in MIP they are supposed to touch; material over the prep is fine), don't register soft tissue (it moves in the mouth but not in stone), and if missing teeth don't allow a stable mounting, use a record base. Two reasons a registration, whatever the material, rarely fits even when trimmed: the material's resilience, and detail greater than the stone cast's. Occlusion is measured in microns; 20 µm off and the crown is out of occlusion. Used with care, VPS can be very accurate; otherwise it adds error. Trim windows so you can see the cusps seat.

Five requirements of interocclusal records (Dawson): 1. the record must not move teeth or displace soft tissue; 2. its accuracy must be verifiable in the mouth; 3. it must fit the casts as accurately as it fits the mouth; 4. its accuracy must be verifiable on the casts; 5. it must not distort in storage or transport to the lab.

Eccentric records and programming the articulator

Eccentric records program the articulator to follow the patient's condylar movement. They are most meaningful when mounted in CR (bilateral balanced occlusion in dentures, reorganized treatment). The protrusive record: the mandible moves forward from CR 3-5 mm, without lateral deviation; one record sets the SCI on both sides. Lateral records: the mandible moves in laterotrusion 3-5 mm; you need two (left and right working motion), and each sets the contralateral SCI and the contralateral medial-wall settings (Bennett angle and immediate side shift): a right lateral record sets the left side.

Protrusive records are preferred. The SCI measured with a lateral record (down the medial wall) is steeper than the SCI from a protrusive record (down the articular eminence). If the goal is posterior disclusion, contacts that are avoided in protrusion will also miss in right and left laterotrusion, so the shallower protrusive SCI is the safer setting: if the articulator is shallower than the patient, the patient just gets more disclusion; if it is steeper, the restoration may hit. For the same reason many clinicians set an arbitrary 30°: most patients' protrusive angles range from about 20 to 60° (commonly 35-40°), so a 30° setting gives decent anatomy and still discludes in the mouth (20° makes the cusps too shallow). For a bilateral balanced denture you would do the opposite; that comes later.

Why 3-5 mm? Beyond that the condyle's path is curving and the teeth are separated anyway. The orbiting condyle's path curves, so the Bennett angle measured depends on where the record is taken: at 3-5 mm of condylar movement the angle is larger; at 7-10 mm it is smaller, which builds narrower fossae on the posterior teeth and more likely interferences.

To program: release the centric latch and loosen the settings (both SCIs for a protrusive record; the contralateral SCI and the Bennett and side-shift settings for a lateral); seat the record on the upper cast and the lower cast into it; the condylar element now touches neither the superior fossa nor the medial wall; adjust the SCI until the element touches the superior fossa surface, then tighten (a protrusive record is done here); for a lateral record, adjust the Bennett angle and/or immediate side shift until the medial wall touches the element, tighten, and repeat with the other side's record.

Semi-adjustable articulators adapt to patient-specific condylar movement, a significant advantage over non-adjustable ones. They take more time, "but well worth the effort," because they minimize intraoral adjustment, and they cost more. Some models (including the Denar 320, calibrated) are interchangeable: mounted casts move between articulators without losing accuracy, so the articulator doesn't travel to the lab (Oral Arts keeps calibrated Denar 320s), fewer articulators are needed and less damage happens. As a resident, before interchangeability, he used 17 articulators to run his cases.

Fully adjustable articulators

The most sophisticated instruments in dentistry for reproducing mandibular movement, with precise adjustments for the condylar inclination (lateral and protrusive paths separately, not just sagittal), the Bennett angle and immediate lateral shift (curved or custom paths, not straight), the rotating condyle (its small superior-inferior and anterior-posterior motion affects cusp height and fossa depth on the working side) and the intercondylar distance (not everyone is 4 inches; it changes the eccentric paths of opposing cusps, so the groove and ridge positions). The Denar D5A is one; the Denar 330 is a semi-adjustable that comes close.
