Programming them takes complex procedures: 1. the exact hinge axis with a kinematic facebow (a hinge-axis locator: the upper bow holds a grid, the lower a stylus; hinge the mandible in CR and adjust the stylus until it only rotates; the point was once tattooed on the skin); 2. dynamic capture of mandibular movement, because positional records can't show it: the pantograph captures the "timing" of movement, with a lower bow carrying 6 recording tables and an upper bow 6 styli, the teeth separated by a central bearing device so they can't influence the motion, through protrusive and right and left laterotrusive movements, then transferred to the articulator and adjusted until it reproduces the tracings (hours of work); 3. a CR record. Today's jaw-tracking systems (SAM Axioquick, ModJaw 4D, Whip Mix Cadiax, KaVo Protar, the 3Shape Trios's patient-specific motion) capture the same thing in minutes and feed a virtual articulator. Any record is influenced by the patient knowing it is being taken, so practice and relaxation help.

Record thickness. On a fully adjustable articulator the exact hinge axis is captured, so the arc of opening and closing in terminal hinge movement is the same on the patient and the articulator, and the thickness of the CR record doesn't affect accuracy. On a semi-adjustable articulator the arbitrary facebow gives an AHA that only estimates the PHA, so the arcs differ and the thicker the record, the more error. So on a semi-adjustable: make CR records with minimal thickness, or at the vertical dimension you intend to treat, where the two arcs meet and the articulator is "dead on."

The major advantage of a fully adjustable articulator is duplicating the patient, in the hope of minimal intraoral adjustment. The disadvantages: time-consuming, technique-sensitive instrumentation and significant expense. In the analog world that hope rarely came true; digital workflows are making the concept a reality.

Selecting an articulator

1. The patient's occlusion. Anterior guidance usually predominates in eccentric tooth contact, because it is closer to the teeth. With strong anterior guidance, a less sophisticated articulator can be used for posterior teeth (a crown on #20 will disclude). With poor anterior guidance (little vertical or horizontal overlap, malaligned or missing teeth, pathology; skeletal Class II arch discrepancies, edge-to-edge Class III), the posterior determinant controls more of the movement and a more sophisticated articulator is needed. It is hard to justify a non-adjustable articulator for any tooth that is part of the anterior guidance.

2. The extent of the restorative work. The more the articulator mimics the patient, the less intraoral adjustment. Minor procedures can use simpler instruments; complex reconstruction (a four-unit bridge from #22 to #18 replaces half the posterior occlusion) needs more sophisticated ones. "The job dictates the tool, not the other way around." 3. The limits of the articulator system, in how much intraoral adjustment will be needed. 4. The skill of the clinician: "A semi-adjustable articulator in the hands of a knowledgeable clinician may be of greater assistance in treatment than a fully adjustable articulator in the hands of an inexperienced operator" (add to that, a careless one), and if the records are careless or the casts inaccurately mounted, any articulator loses its usefulness.

His selection table, in short: a restoration discluded significantly by anterior guidance can go on any of the three; a restoration that is minimally discluded (eccentric interferences likely), part of the anterior guidance, one of several units, crossing the midline, with a change of VDO, a diagnostic CR mounting, steep or flat eminence, acute or flat curve of Spee, a steep occlusal plane or anatomic cusp height all call for at least a semi-adjustable (a fully adjustable does them best). The non-adjustable wins only on ease of lab use (expense) and ease of clinician use. "Anything that you can do in the laboratory that saves you clinic time is well worth the investment."
full.malocclusion:
What's tested
  • The functional disturbance model: normal function + an event greater than physiologic tolerance gives symptoms
  • What a TMD is (and isn't): a collective term, about half muscle and a third joint, not the same as orofacial pain
  • The five etiologies: mandibular stability, trauma, emotional stress, deep pain input, parafunctional activity
  • Orthopedic vs occlusal stability; orthopedic instability and its risk factors; what the evidence says about occlusion and TMD
  • Occlusal interferences, the "high crown" and protective co-contraction; why prophylactic equilibration isn't supported
  • Occlusal therapy: reversible vs irreversible, splints, the rule of thirds, conservative first
  • Trauma: the five force factors, normal and pathologic mobility, Miller's index; the four mechanisms of wear and the erosion patterns
  • Bruxism: centrally mediated, not started by occlusion, treated by protecting the teeth with a splint

On 10/29 Dr. Givan took "a different direction in occlusion": why occlusion is a real problem for so many dentists, where things don't work, and what we do about it. This lecture lays the groundwork for the third-year TMD course. Sometimes the occlusion has nothing to do with a patient's problem; other times, working on the occlusion helps the patient toward a good outcome even though it wasn't part of the cause. When a student asked whether every condition on the TMD classification list would be tested, he said to look for the general themes: the individual entities are the third-year course, and apart from one or two (such as local muscle soreness) he would not go into them in detail this year.

Normal function and dysfunction

The normal functions of the masticatory system are chewing, swallowing and speaking. Dysfunction is the alteration or inhibition of normal function. It usually shows up as an inability to move the way we should (can't chew, can't swallow), or as pain, which can be intense, severe and not easily treated.

Dysfunction results from a functional disturbance: the functional disturbance is the cause, and often we don't know why it happened. Examples of dysfunction: muscle disorders (decreased range of motion; an acute malocclusion from a change in the resting length of the muscles); structural changes in the joint (deviations on opening or closure); occlusal overload associated with tooth fracture, pulpal pain, periodontal bone loss and tooth wear (most periodontal bone loss is from infection, but force plays a role); and headache. There are over 250 kinds of headache, and treating each may take something different.

What a TMD is

Patients say they "have TMJ," but the TMJ is the joint; the correct term is a temporomandibular disorder (TMD). A TMD is a collective term embracing a number of clinical problems that involve the masticatory muscles, the TMJ, or both. It is not one thing: it is a collection of different clinical entities (over 40), each different, and this has been one of the real problems in how dentistry has tried to treat "TMD patients." What they have in common is that most alter normal function and some, but not always, cause pain of varied severity.

General types: problems in the muscles, maybe 50%; problems in the joints, maybe 35%; others (vascular, neurologic and more), and often combinations. The classification on the slides is Bell's, older but widely used, with four groups: masticatory muscle disorders; TMJ disorders (how the condyle and disc fit together, structural changes from development or trauma, and inflammatory disorders such as arthritis, retrodiscitis and synovitis); chronic mandibular hypomobility (ankylosis, contracture); and growth disorders. Every one of them is diagnosed and treated differently, so "I'm being treated for a TMD" tells you almost nothing. Myofascial pain, by contrast, is one specific TMD with its own features, such as trigger points. Many TMDs have nothing to do with occlusion, but all may be a functional disturbance.

A TMD is not synonymous with orofacial pain, a much larger category of disorders of the head and neck that includes TMDs and other pains outside the masticatory structures. Pain also depends on how we interpret the world around us, so some of these problems are physical and some biopsychosocial.

Dentistry has historically tied occlusion to TMD, which isn't a good thing to do, because occlusion doesn't relate to many of these entities. Why the tie? Things we do in the mouth often help. As he put it, "here's the way I'll say it in 2026": the occlusal work helps provide an environment of healing that helps resolve other disorders. Being a helpful adjunct does not make occlusion part of the cause.

How a functional disturbance develops

The model: Normal function + Event > Physiologic tolerance ⇒ Symptoms.

Normal function. Chewing, swallowing and speaking are regulated by the brainstem (the central pattern generator and its engrams), influenced by peripheral sensory and nociceptive input (bite on something uncomfortable and a response happens) and by CNS effects such as the limbic system, which stress and behavior turn up or down.

Events. Local events: a high crown or filling, tissue trauma (pizza that was too hot), muscle strain, blunt trauma or repeated microtrauma, bruxism, constant (deep) pain input; in fact any change in a sensory or proprioceptive input. Systemic events: emotions, stress, and feeling bad all over with the flu.

Physiologic tolerance is the ability to tolerate an event, and it is affected by many factors. Local: the occlusion of the teeth defines a position of the mandible, which affects the joints, muscles, ligaments and orthopedic posture; an unstable orthopedic relationship of the mandible to the maxilla and cranial base. Systemic: genetics, gender, diet, acute or chronic disease.

If normal function plus the event stays below the physiologic tolerance, the patient adapts and has no symptoms; most of the time we tolerate things fairly well. If it exceeds the tolerance, symptoms begin. Each element of the model can change, and an event tolerated on one day may not be tolerable on another. That is the story you hear from TMD patients again and again: fine all their life until last Monday, then on Tuesday intense pain, and you rarely know what changed. There is no sticker on anyone's forehead saying how much they will tolerate.

When the tolerances of the masticatory system are exceeded, structures break down. The signs and symptoms: a. pulpitis (or hypersensitive teeth), b. tooth wear or fracture, c. tooth mobility, d. masticatory muscle pain, e. TMJ pain, f. ear pain, g. headache pain.

The five etiologies of functional disturbances

The list isn't complete, but these five are common: 1. mandibular stability, 2. trauma, 3. emotional stress, 4. deep pain input, 5. parafunctional activities. He spent the most time on mandibular stability, because that one is often directly in our hands.

1. Mandibular stability: what the evidence says

Mandibular stability regards the simultaneous fit of the teeth and both joints against the skull. Research shows some relation of occlusion to functional disturbances, but the dental literature rarely says which TMD it studied, so its patient groups are mixed. "When I first learned this 35 years ago, it really hasn't changed a lot today."

Pullinger and Seligman, a well-cited group of studies, noted a higher frequency of these signs in TMD patients: a skeletal anterior open bite, a CO to MIP slide greater than 2 mm, horizontal overjet greater than 4 mm (no good anterior guidance), and five or more missing posterior teeth. But the same signs are found in the non-TMD population, so the authors concluded that occlusion is not the most important factor in TMDs: multiple co-factors were more common.

The textbook's review of 57 epidemiologic studies (Table 7-2): 22 found no relationship and 35 found occlusion related to TMD symptoms. The occlusal conditions varied widely from study to study, they don't always lead to symptoms, a relationship doesn't imply cause, and the studies usually don't specify the type of TMD. Overall, the evidence is lacking.

Orthopedic stability and occlusal stability

Despite the lack of evidence, it is widely accepted that sound occlusal relationships are the basis of successful dentistry: all teeth contact evenly and simultaneously; all contacts are between centric cusp tips and flattened surfaces, directing forces through the long axes; the anterior teeth disclude the posterior teeth (mutually protected occlusion). In patients with temporomandibular problems, following these same principles often helps.

Ideally every part is stably seated: joints fully seated → orthopedic stability; teeth fully in contact (MIP) → occlusal stability. That leads to the treatment goals for the musculoskeletal stable position. For a muscle disorder, an inflammatory disorder or a severely debilitated dentition, provide optimum functional occlusion with the condyles in their most musculoskeletal stable position (centric relation):

1. The condyles rest in their most superior-anterior position against the slopes of the articular eminences. 2. The articular discs are properly interposed between the condyles and fossae (in some disc disorders this can't be achieved). 3. On closure in that position the posterior teeth contact evenly and simultaneously, centric cusp tips on flat surfaces, forces along the long axes. 4. In eccentric movement the anterior teeth contact and disclude the posterior teeth. 5. In the alert feeding position (head forward and down) the posterior contacts are more prominent than the anterior. Because these goals help treat functional disturbances, they also become the goals for permanently restoring the dentition.

With the teeth apart, the muscles seat the joints: orthopedic stability. Keep the joints seated and close until the teeth touch, and in most people the result is occlusal instability: only about 10% have MIP coincident with closure in CR. Dental stability, prioritized for function, will sacrifice orthopedic stability: to bring the teeth into MIP, one or both joints come off their seat.

Orthopedic instability: when the teeth are brought into MIP, one (or both) condyles are not in a stable relationship with the disc and fossa. A stable occlusion with unstable joints may lead to an intracapsular disorder (inside the joint capsule; one of the many TMDs, and a common one). Risk factors: the degree of discrepancy (a condylar misposition of 1-2 mm is not likely to create a problem; over 3 mm presents increased risk, and some would say 4 mm); and the amount of loading (patients who brux have greater risk). A greater risk does not mean the patient will have a problem. So in some circumstances occlusion can contribute to a functional disturbance.

Dental malocclusion does influence function: a poor occlusion doesn't return the mandible to MIP as cleanly, and worn teeth change how we close. There are reports of more TMD with open bite or Angle Class II (a skeletal Class II patient tends to posture the jaw forward and has little anterior guidance), but they are not well supported by the literature. Malocclusion may only become important when considering joint position.

His patient. When he was a resident, a woman came to the clinic in intense pain after seeing many dentists. She had a lot of crown and bridge work and had been fine until, one day, she wasn't. His program director, who listened and understood what was going on, put her in a full-coverage splint, adjusted over months so that all the teeth touched. As the splint let her condyles return to a seated position, an open bite appeared: years of restorations had built her teeth to MIP while moving her farther and farther from orthopedic stability, to keep dental stability. She was held at the new position with the splint, restored in provisionals at that vertical for well over a year, then moved to her final restorations, about two years in all. Was occlusion an issue here? Definitely yes. That is how orthopedic instability can lead to a problem, but in many other TMDs it isn't the case.

Occlusal instability and muscle function

Example 1: unexpected contact. Bite unexpectedly on something hard and you reflexively open: a protective nociceptive reflex, rapid, involuntary and subconscious, in the trigeminal motor nucleus. It is a complex reflex, because opening means shutting down many muscles and activating many others.

Example 2: stimulating the masticatory muscles. From EMG studies: if mediotrusive contacts are eliminated, the masseter and temporalis are not activated by a mediotrusive movement. This supports canine guidance. In the classic study (Manns, 1989), a full-coverage maxillary splint was divided into anterior, premolar (intermediate) and molar (posterior) blocks and the EMG recorded with each. Without posterior contact, muscle activity dropped significantly; adding the molar contacts brought it up to full. Two theories came out of it: 1. anterior tooth contact inhibits muscle contraction; 2. a lack of posterior tooth contact fails to activate muscle contraction. Later studies confirmed the second. Posterior contact stimulates the elevator muscles: bite, crunch, close down. That is how we're wired.

The masticatory muscles have two basic activities. Ortho-function (normal function): elevation, depression, laterotrusion and so on; protective reflexes are present; tooth contacts affect specific muscle groups, and posterior contact stimulates the elevators. Parafunction: clenching, grinding (bruxism) and oral habits. "All bets are off": muscles fire without that feedback from the mouth, agonists and antagonists fight each other, and the hyperactivity raises muscle tonus, giving fatigue and strain. These are very different mechanisms, and they are not influenced by tooth contacts as was once thought.

The "high" crown. You deliver a crown on #19 that is slightly high (the jaw can feel microns). The patient develops protective muscle co-contraction, a TMD of muscle origin: restricted or guarded mandibular movement from co-contraction of the muscles, as a way to avoid pain from the initial event. There is "nothing pathologic about it": it is a normal, healthy avoidance behavior, and the source can be a high crown, a tooth with an endodontic lesion or a burned palate. But moving in ways we don't normally move leads to generalized muscle soreness and pain (local muscle soreness, myalgia). The conclusion: an unstable occlusal contact influenced muscle activity. Does occlusion cause a specific TMD? In this case, yes.

Existing interferences are another matter. Posterior mediotrusive (non-working) and laterotrusive (working) contacts are equally noted in symptomatic and asymptomatic patients: "that's a very important point." A CO-MIP slide under 2 mm has equal incidence in both groups; over 2 mm, the incidence increases in symptomatic patients; interferences to maximum closure are more common in symptomatic patients. Incidence does not prove causality.

Summary. Altering an occlusal contact does influence muscle activity. Introducing an interference can lead to pain or dysfunction. Eliminating existing interferences does not seem to significantly alter the symptoms of TMD. Limited data suggest an interference-free occlusion is associated with a lower incidence of TMD symptoms developing. Current practice: equilibrating a patient's occlusion for prevention is not supported. So when you deliver a crown or a filling, avoid putting in a mediotrusive contact, because that's too sudden a change; but if the patient already had one, taking it away is probably not going to change their symptoms. The precise effect of occlusal stability on symptoms hasn't been established: sometimes related, sometimes not. A better question: does CNS posturing of the mandible anteriorly or anterolaterally to MIP increase risk as a co-factor for muscle and joint disorders?

To sum up occlusion and functional disturbances: acute changes produce protective co-contraction, but most often new engrams develop with little consequence once the interference is resolved. Orthopedic instability must be considerable to matter, and it needs loading forces (such as parafunction) to destabilize. Occlusal problems that weren't a problem before may become one if an event finally exceeds the tolerance, or the tolerance changes: "the straw that broke the camel's back." Two general statements, explored in the TMD course, with exceptions: problems bringing the teeth together (mandibular movement) are often manifested in the muscles; once the teeth are in occlusion, problems with applying force are often manifested in the joints.

Occlusal therapy to establish stability

Occlusal therapy is a general term for any treatment that alters a patient's occlusal condition. It can be reversible (non-invasive or temporary) or irreversible (invasive or permanent). Occlusal therapies are used for many dental needs (caries, esthetics); here the subject is the smaller group of patients with a functional disturbance, where you think changing the occlusion matters.

ReversibleIrreversible (all change the occlusal relationships)
Patient educationOcclusal equilibration
Physical therapy (self or professional assist)Restorative dentistry
PharmacotherapyRepositioning splint
CounselingOrthodontics
Flat plane stabilization splint (the one that changes occlusal stability)Orthognathic surgery, arthroscopy, open joint surgery

Splint therapy treats muscle pain, protects teeth and restorations (for example in bruxism), alleviates joint pain (less force into the joint) and is part of trial therapy. The splint is a plastic covering over the occlusal surfaces with a new occlusal surface built on it: whatever MIP was, it's gone. The goal of a stabilization splint is to have the joints seated and new contacts against the plastic. It is "hugely effective," so effective it led dentistry to conclude occlusion must be the problem. Not the case.

Splints can be maxillary or mandibular, full or partial arch, and stabilizing or repositioning. A stabilizing splint provides occlusal (dental) stability while the joints are seated in an orthopedically stable relationship. A repositioning splint is used in disc displacements, sleep apnea and other cases where a specific non-centric mandibular position is wanted. Many names: occlusal splints, devices or appliances, night guards, anterior bite plates, posterior pivots.

Both maxillary and mandibular splints can provide a perfect dental occlusion coinciding with orthopedic stability. A maxillary splint has a posterior flat plane (no indentations or elevations, so no eccentric contacts) with an anterior ramp; it is very stable and retentive, sturdier and less likely to fracture (better for heavy clenchers), easier to get anterior contacts on and to adjust, usable in Class I, II and even III, and ideally suited for Class II division 1 (excessive horizontal overlap). It is visible, so normally for nighttime. A mandibular splint (its ramp behind the front teeth) causes less speech interference and is less visible when speaking, so it is preferable for daytime wear; he makes many for athletes.

Full coverage covers all the teeth in the arch, reduces the chance of teeth moving and is recommended in almost all situations: by far the most effective splint, and patients in pain want to keep it in. Partial coverage may let covered teeth intrude and uncovered teeth extrude (supereruption), may not be as effective, and small ones can be an aspiration hazard at night; whether they are easier to wear is questionable.

Irreversible treatment. Without a functional disturbance, irreversible treatment for broken, decayed or missing teeth is simply the bulk of the dental care dentists provide. If a functional disturbance is present, irreversible occlusal treatment is only indicated when sufficient evidence suggests the primary etiologic factor is the mandibular instability (the occlusal condition): you can't ungrind a tooth. In general, perform the least amount of dental alteration that fulfills the treatment goal, and choose the type of therapy by the severity of the malocclusion.

Selective grinding (equilibration, occlusal adjustment) is minor reshaping of enamel surfaces; avoid exposing dentin and creating iatrogenic sensitivity (if it would reach dentin, restore instead). Technique: 1. eliminate prematurities (contacts on initial closure), 2. eliminate interferences (contacts blocking a movement), 3. direct centric forces axially, 4. establish optimum occlusion (details in the textbook). When the interarch alignment deviates farther from ideal, grinding would expose dentin or mutilate the teeth, so use fixed prosthetics and minor orthodontics (properly done, Invisalign can act as splint and tooth movement at once). Major deviations from ideal interarch relations need orthodontics, orthognathic surgery and prosthetics.

The rule of thirds simplifies the choice: mark the contacts with the condyles in the desired position; if the discrepancy falls in the first third of the tooth, selective grinding; the middle third, minor orthodontics and fixed prosthetics (most deviations are here); beyond that, major orthodontics, orthognathic surgery and prosthetics.

Success. The evidence is weak: a lack of scientific evidence relating therapy to effects (the standard is the double-blind clinical trial), a lack of agreement on TMD diagnostic categories, and some causal factors are hard to control (emotional stress). Long-term success of reversible and irreversible treatments is similar, 50-90%. So the treatment philosophy: because conservative treatment reports similar success, it is the first attempt; non-conservative treatment is attempted if conservative approaches fail. Other factors in the choice: symptoms, condition of the dentition, systemic health, esthetics and finances. A splint is cheap and easy, but a patient can't chew and eat with it all their life.

Consider the population in four groups: no dental treatment needed and TMD asymptomatic (the basic hygiene patient); dental treatment needed, TMD asymptomatic (the bulk of patients, "where we make our living"); TMD symptomatic, no dental treatment needed; and the "red light" group: TMD symptomatic and needing a lot of dental treatment, where guidance is hardest.

2. Trauma

"A force is only traumatic when it produces trauma." What makes a force (occlusal, external) traumatic is characterized by five factors: 1. magnitude (how great), 2. frequency (how often), 3. duration (how long it acts), 4. direction (we handle vertical forces well, horizontal forces poorly), 5. distribution (how many teeth resist it; for example posterior bite collapse). Combined, these may lead to dysfunction.

Types of trauma: macrotrauma, a sudden force resulting in structural alterations (auto accidents, acceleration-deceleration injuries); microtrauma, small repetitive forces over time (for example bruxism). Common outcomes: orthopedic trauma (a broken jaw), intracapsular disorders (a blow to the side of the face), and direct damage to the teeth and alveolus: cracks and fractures, mobility, and wear.

Occlusal trauma may produce histologic changes: injury to the PDL, bone resorption, cemental changes, vascular injury, pulpal hyperemia (questioned). Clinical findings: tooth mobility, tooth migration, attrition, widening of the PDL, tenderness to pressure, pulpal pain, and flattening of the TM joint (controversial). Where: the attachment apparatus (the PDL and adjacent structures) is the usual site; the gingiva and mucosa rarely. Recall that the stability of the connective tissue attachment, affected by inflammatory and not occlusal factors, determines whether bone loss may be reversible.

Tooth mobility

Vertical mobility is related to the root's surface area and shape. A healthy tooth shows no clinically observable vertical mobility, but the actual initial vertical movement is about 28 µm, the same for anterior and posterior teeth. The immediate rebound is about 7 µm, and full recovery takes almost 4 hours. An implant moves only 2-3 µm under a 10-lb force, from the viscoelastic strain of the bony interface: the reason implant occlusion is handled differently.

Horizontal mobility is always greater than vertical. Single-rooted teeth are more mobile than multi-rooted, and the amount depends on the width of the PDL, the root attachment area, the elasticity of the alveolus and the function (position) of the tooth. A force of about 500 g moves a tooth horizontally 56 to 108 µm; 150 µm is the limit of physiologic horizontal mobility, and beyond it mobility is abnormal or pathologic, an outcome of a functional disturbance. Mobility changes through the day: greatest on arising from sleep, least late in the day after function.

Adapted mobility: the tissues adapt or cope and the changes are not progressive; the increased mobility is self-limiting, and a tooth may stay that way for years. Traumatic mobility: the adaptive capacity (biological tolerance) is exceeded, and the mobility increases progressively; this is an indication for splinting the teeth (more surface area to resist the force). To tell them apart you must monitor over time: increasing mobility needs treatment; stable mobility is less of an indication.

Miller's Mobility Index (1938): the tooth is held firmly between two instruments and moved back and forth. 0, no detectable movement; 1, barely distinguishable movement; 2, any horizontal movement up to 1 mm; 3, more than 1 mm, or depressed or rotated (vertical movement). The scale has been modified many times.

Dental wear

Wear dates from recent to prehistoric times, when an abrasive diet (food ground with stones) was the usual cause. Physiologic wear is wear acceptable for the patient's age (a 75-year-old has chewed for 60 years); the same wear at 30 is not. Pain is usually not a symptom: wear is too slow. Patients usually seek treatment for esthetics, and by then an easy treatment is usually too late. If wear is pathologic, treatment is indicated; it won't get better on its own.

Treatment: best before the wear extends to multiple teeth (twenty worn teeth at about $1,200 a crown is very expensive). The canines and incisors involved in anterior guidance are often the first to wear (early signs); without guidance, posterior wear can be significant because forces increase toward the back. Severe wear may need crown lengthening, endodontics or orthodontic extrusion before prosthodontics. General rule: if 3 mm of tooth structure is coronal to the papilla, crown lengthening is often not indicated.

MechanismWhat it isWhat you see
AttritionTooth-to-tooth grinding from normal or parafunctional activity (often bruxism)Facets match and are only at occlusal contacts; shiny with sharp edges; enamel and dentin in the facet at the same height
Abrasion"Third-body wear": mechanical raking of a foreign material; habitualFood particles, chewing tobacco; most common is toothbrush-assisted wear
Erosion"Chemically assisted wear": acid dissolution, intrinsic (gastric acid) or extrinsic (food and drink acid)Extends beyond the occlusal contacts; dull facets; cupping (dentin wears faster than enamel); "proud restorations" standing above the eroded tooth
AbfractionLoss of tooth structure from flexural biomechanical loading (Latin, "to break away")A notch near the CEJ, usually facial; saliva may add "stress corrosion"

Wear mechanisms frequently act together, and the presence of acid accelerates mechanical wear. (In class he said that with erosion alone the facets don't match each other, because it isn't a tooth-to-tooth contact.) Many extrinsic acids also carry sucrose, adding a caries problem.

Erosion patterns. GERD: the classic appearance is erosion on the lingual of all the maxillary teeth to the second molars and the occlusal surfaces of the mandibular molars; often asymmetrical, because in sleep the refluxed acid rolls off the tongue onto the lingual surfaces and patients have a preferred side to sleep on (on the back, both sides). Bulimia nervosa (recurrent binge eating followed by purging, fasting, laxatives, enemas, diuretics or over-exercising): erosion mostly on the maxillary anterior teeth, sometimes to the first premolar, posterior teeth only when long-standing; the maxillary anteriors can be completely destroyed while the mandibular anteriors are not (protected by the tongue and saliva). Carbonated beverage abuse: pattern 1, swish and hold in the vestibule to fizz, then swallow, giving generalized erosion with a satin appearance and islands of exposed dentin; pattern 2, pooling the drink in the back of the mouth to fizz and cool, very severe, with high caries and more wear on the back and front teeth. Citrus fruit abuse: type 1, biting fruit and sucking the juice through the teeth, erodes the front teeth to a "screwdriver" appearance; type 2, biting and chewing on the molars, looks like beverage pooling, with more posterior wear. Less common: drug abuse (aspirin, meth), swimming (chlorinated water, on the side they breathe on) and occupational exposure (battery and galvanizing workers).

Noncarious cervical lesions (NCCLs) are one of the most common demineralization diseases in the body: a cervical defect either smooth, rounded and saucer-like (growing more in height) or a sharp V-shaped notch (growing in height and depth). Caries is often not present but can develop (arrest it with silver diamine fluoride). Prevalence varies in the literature from 10% to 90%, but all accept it increases with age. They are found throughout the mouth, most often on the facial surfaces of maxillary premolars; lingual lesions occur but are rarely severe. Treatment with resin composite is typically delayed until necessary: progression, sensitivity or quality of life, poor esthetics, food collection. The etiology is multifactorial: excessive horizontal toothbrushing, acidic foods and drinks, reflux disease; occlusal factors are associated but not sufficient alone. The concept of abfraction (tensile fatigue flexing the cervical area under occlusal load, separating enamel rods, with saliva inducing "stress corrosion") is supported by in vitro studies, but clinical documentation has neither validated nor rejected it, so it isn't included as a primary mechanism of wear. Clenching, nail biting and a diagnosis of TMD are significantly associated with NCCLs, and the sustained loads of clenching and nail biting are more damaging to mineralized tissue than the dynamic, shifting loads of bruxism.

3. Emotional stress and 4. deep pain input

Emotional stress. The emotional centers influence muscle function through the hypothalamus, the reticular system and the limbic system. For example, gamma efferents stimulate the intrafusal fibers of the muscle spindles to contract, "sensitizing" the muscle and raising its tonicity, often in the head and neck. (The muscle spindle is the major sensory organ of muscle: intrafusal fibers, innervated by gamma efferents, lie parallel to the extrafusal fibers and sense the change in muscle length and velocity.) In that state almost anything, such as an unexpected passive stretch, is perceived as pain. That's the physiologic reason you feel tight and worn out after three weeks of studying for an occlusion test.

Deep pain input (deep is anything below the skin or mucosa; superficial is on it) is often overlooked. Example: limited opening with odontogenic pain; resolve the pulpal problem (an extraction, say) and the opening returns to normal. Remote pain, such as cervical pain, may affect the masticatory system, and referred pain is covered next year. We don't chew, speak and swallow the same way when we hurt. Nociception also inhibits motor output (a guarded protection of damaged tissue), so altered pathways must be activated to keep functioning.

5. Parafunctional activities

Parafunctional activities are movements outside normal function. They can lead to a functional disturbance, and because they are subconscious they are difficult to manage.

Daytime (diurnal): clenching (often tied to stress; these patients often have a history of fractured, chipped, broken or splayed teeth, and tori or exostoses are common); grinding (by different mechanisms than at night); oral habits (cheek and tongue biting, finger and thumb sucking); unusual postural habits; occupational habits (biting pencils, pens or nails; holding a telephone or violin under the chin). Nighttime (nocturnal): bruxism, rhythmic contractions causing clenching and grinding during sleep; tongue compression (can move teeth, and leaves a scalloped lateral border of the tongue); cheek biting.

Bruxism is very damaging. Compared with function (Table 7-3, Okeson), its forces are often three to five times greater, they are horizontal rather than down the long axis, the mandible can be in any position (eventually MIP itself is worn away), the muscles work differently, and the protective reflexes are absent because we are asleep. Sleep phases come from EEG monitoring: about 80% non-REM (physical rest) and 20% REM (psychic rest). Bruxism is associated with a change from a deeper to a lighter phase of sleep (arousal phases); in research, flashing lights, sound or touch can induce a grinding event. Duration varies: most bruxers have many short events of 5-10 seconds (the slides total 12-40 minutes a night), and patients vary in how much damage they show.

Causes of bruxism. Bruxism is centrally mediated (CNS): probably more related to something like restless leg syndrome than to the occlusion. Besides the changes in sleep phase, there is a relationship to oxygen saturation (an association with sleep apnea). It is influenced by emotional stress, medications and genetic predisposition. Occlusion? Recent studies do not support that occlusal contact initiates bruxism events as was once thought.

The primary treatment is a stabilization splint. Placing it gives a temporary cessation of bruxism (a temporary muscle discoordination; in class he said a couple of days to a couple of weeks, the slides say weeks to months), and then the bruxism returns, because it is centrally mediated. So the goal is to brux against the splint and preserve the teeth: "brux against the $400 splint and avoid the $40,000 rehab." There is no cure. Additional recommendations, with little supporting evidence: sleeping on the side, stress management, avoiding alcohol, smoking cessation, hypnosis, acupuncture.

Stress and muscle activity. Rugh's data tracked nighttime masseter EMG over days against life events: activity rose with a job interview, a fight with a parent or quitting a job, and fell on a vacation in Hawaii; stress, pain and nocturnal muscle activity were well correlated. Patients bring baggage you often don't know about, which is why the TMD course stresses a multidisciplinary approach: other health care providers help with things a dentist can't.

Bruxism in children is common (it can sound like a thousand violins) and is not considered to be associated with symptoms. It seems related to the developing dentition looking for occlusal stability, a different mechanism. Tell concerned parents it is often benign and to monitor; if masticatory function is affected, the child should be evaluated by a dentist. Most of those teeth are primary teeth and will be lost.

His close: occlusion matters significantly in a few of these disorders, but the vast majority have nothing to do with it. Yet for most of them a simple stabilization splint provides an environment of healing that helps resolve the symptoms. It is not treating the etiology, and it doesn't mean occlusion was the cause. Next week: removable (denture) occlusion, ahead of the denture course in January.

On 11/5 Dr. Givan took "a different turn": occlusion on dentures. He is required to present it before the class has had its denture course (that starts in January, with him), so he stepped back to explain what a denture is and how it works. The whole goal is different from the dentate patient: with removable occlusion the goal is to keep the prosthesis in the mouth and have some kind of function. A complete denture is fabricated from fairly sophisticated plastics and essentially floats on the tissues: no connection, no attachment. Patients who call them "my upper plate and my lower plate" aren't wrong: picture a plate from your cabinet trying to stay in position in someone's mouth. If occlusion is bringing the jaws together, how the dentures fit together decides whether they stay in.

Denture words

Denture teeth are not teeth: no pulp, no enamel or dentin, no biology, just a tooth-colored piece of plastic that mimics a tooth. They are attached to a plastic denture base, the part that fits over the tissues; how well the base is adapted to the tissues plays a large role in how well the denture stays in. The extensions that come up into the vestibule on each side are the denture flange, and the extent of the flange, as far as it can go before reaching the boundary between moving and non-moving tissues, is the peripheral border.

A patient with no teeth is edentulous; fully edentulous means none remain. Their dentures are complete dentures or full dentures, as opposed to partial dentures, when some teeth are present. The terms aren't great, he admits, but they are what we have.

When teeth are lost, the bone goes away: resorption. Patients who have lost a lot of it find it very hard to eat and keep up their nutrition, particularly with the lower jaw. That problem, edentulism, is what drove the development of dental implants almost 50 years ago: "we must have dental implants in order to be able to retain a denture." It wasn't the single-tooth implant or the fixed hybrid that drove it.

A short history: what role did occlusion play?

"What do I really want you to know from this is essentially... what was the role of occlusion in this? And you're going to find out the answer will be practically none." The history slides are all marked "No test questions": know the point, not the names and dates.

The earliest dentures were carved, from wood and later ivory, before impressions or models existed, and they were made mostly for esthetics: people felt they looked better with teeth. A few have knobs at the back that suggest an attempt at chewing surfaces, but there was no real occlusion. In the 1600s and 1700s, carved ivory prostheses had hinges or springs at the back for opening and closing (ivory breaks down in the mouth too). You couldn't really speak or eat with them; they were for those who could afford them. Pierre Fauchard, the father of dentistry, published a design for a carved ivory denture with flexible metal springs: again, not functional. By the late 1600s impressions could be taken in beeswax and poured in plaster of Paris, so pieces could be made to come on and off.

George Washington's teeth were not wooden. His dentist, John Greenwood, made several sets, carved from ox bone and ivory, many with a swaged gold base and springs at the back. Both George and Martha Washington had the same complaints denture wearers have today: their letters to Greenwood, in the Reynolds Historical Library at UAB, say it hurts here on the side and is uncomfortable to eat and talk. Washington was a man of few words, and it isn't surprising why.

Dentures came to fit well enough to use a little suction: James Gardette found that a well-fitting base is held by atmospheric pressure. It is still one way we keep a maxillary denture in (occasionally a mandibular one), though the first sip of a hot liquid breaks it. Human teeth taken from corpses were used for a time ("not our most ethical day in dentistry"), and bases were made of materials such as cellulose that didn't hold up. Then came porcelain: Duchâteau's porcelain dentures (about 1774) chipped and looked too white, and in 1808 Fonzi made individually fired porcelain teeth, his "terro-metallic incorruptible" teeth, that could stay in the mouth without breaking down. Claudius Ash's teeth became popular, with occlusal holes, dots and ridges that didn't mimic human anatomy.

Bonwill made the first real attempt at denture occlusion: he designed teeth to meet a function, arranging arbitrarily formed molds so they kept contact in motion, and set them to his equilateral triangle, the origin of the occlusal plane, with the idea that if the teeth stayed touching all the time, the denture would stay in the mouth. No springs or wires from upper to lower. That is why he is known as the father of articulation. Bases improved too: vulcanite, rubber cross-linked with sulfur, was hugely popular (and dental labs, smelling of sulfur, were something you didn't want to live next to), and tooth and lab industries grew.

Ideas about what the teeth should look like weren't well understood. The temperamental theory, going back to antiquity, held that denture teeth should follow the patient's personality or temperament; it was widely accepted and poorly understood, and it is still with us: denture molds are still described as bold or soft. J. Leon Williams' geometric forms said to shape the teeth like the patient's face: ovoid, square or tapered, also still used today. By the early 20th century more science was applied: Alfred Gysi, working with the Dentists' Supply Company (later Dentsply), perfected balanced occlusion, designing teeth that follow the motion of the mandible to keep the teeth together in bilateral balance, and was the first to use a central bearing device. His Trubyte teeth, from the 1910s, are still sold by Dentsply, among the best-selling denture teeth for over 125 years.

So the history of denture occlusion has nothing to do with the things we talk about for the dentate mouth: where the forces go, posterior disclusion, anterior guidance. With a denture, the goal is to keep it from tipping out of the mouth. Balance refers to countering those tipping motions.

Why denture occlusion is different

We still want the edentulous patient to chew, speak and swallow. But years of developing neuromuscular function with the natural teeth are not on your side: the proprioception of the teeth and alveolar tissues is gone, and patients have only a vague sense of where they are. In many ways a patient with dentures has one upper tooth and one lower tooth: the denture teeth never operate independently; an upper prosthesis and a lower prosthesis work together.

So the arrangement of the denture teeth is all about preventing tipping of the denture when the teeth are brought into contact. That is the whole goal of balancing: "balancing being contrasted as the opposite of tipping." If, in a right working movement, there is contact on both the right and the left side at the same time, the denture won't tip out, and it stays in better function. Those are balancing contacts, the very contacts we avoid in natural teeth.

How a denture stays in the mouth

Physical forces. The slides sort them. Contributing less: atmospheric pressure, vacuum, adhesion, cohesion and the seating force. Contributing more: the interposed fluid, the film of saliva between the base and the tissues (its flow, its viscosity and how thin the film is), and surface tension at the periphery. They depend on the patient's saliva (viscous or thin; it changes with age, and most denture patients are older) and on extension to the periphery: a good border seal keeps air from seeping under the denture and letting it drop or tip. All of them require good adaptation and a border seal. On a cone beam CT of a patient wearing a denture, dark spaces between the base and the tissues show misfit, and where there is misfit, suction and cohesion become almost impossible to capture. And most of them are undone in function, especially by hot liquids: even with good fit, they aren't strong enough to hold a denture while the patient chews.

Muscle control. What really keeps a denture in is the musculature. Some patients develop neuromuscular control that keeps even the worst-fitting denture in place, and they eat fine; others can't manage the best denture you could make. "Muscle control is likely to be the most important factor to keep a denture in place." And remember: most of the time patients have their teeth apart, so adhesion, cohesion and muscle control are what hold the denture then. Two more points from the slides: undercuts in the ridge help only a little, and they can make the denture painful; and an ill-fitting denture makes resorption worse.

What resists tipping, and what makes it harder

Structures have to be in the way to keep a denture from moving, and as they are lost, it gets harder. The slides list what resists tipping. Anatomy: the ridge height, ridge width and ridge shape, the depth of the palatal vault ("a big one for the maxillary denture") and the type of posterior palatal seal. Denture design: the fit of the intaglio surface, the side that rests on the tissues, and occluding contacts that don't move the denture. You will assess the anatomy in the denture course. Some tissues are more compressible than others, particularly toward the soft palate. Because heat-processed resin shrinks, a posterior palatal seal is added at the back to push into the soft tissues and overcome the shrinkage; milled dentures fit intimately enough that it isn't always needed.

"If you always remember this: all removable is movable." Every removable prosthesis has some motion, and we design it to resist that motion. The soft tissues under it vary in thickness and are resilient, so every time the teeth hit, the tissue sinks a little and the denture moves. That is why the occlusion often can't be developed in the mouth: it is built and adjusted outside the mouth, on an articulator. Hanau called this tissue effect the Realeff, short for "resiliency and like effect" (the slides also write "resilient and like effect"); it has been known in dentistry for over a century.

Resorption follows patterns. The maxilla resorbs up and in, so its supporting arch gets smaller than the original arch; the mandible resorbs down and out, so at the level where the teeth are supposed to be, the edentulous mandible becomes larger than the dentate one. The slides give the direction for each region:

RegionAfter the teeth are lost, the bone resorbs
Maxillary anteriorUpward and toward the posterior (inward)
Maxillary posteriorUpward and toward the midline
Mandibular anteriorDownward and toward the anterior (forward)
Mandibular posteriorDownward and away from the midline (outward)

Denture teeth are generally set near where the ridge is ("not rocket science"), so we often have to set them in crossbite, and that's fine: there's nothing wrong with a crossbite in a denture. The jaws also started out different sizes. A skeletal Class I (orthognathic) relationship has the jaws roughly matched in size and shape; in skeletal Class II (retrognathic) the mandible is smaller and set back; skeletal Class III (prognathic) is the opposite. These are related to Angle's molar classes. A patient who becomes a skeletal Class III because the mandible resorbs outward while the maxilla resorbs inward has a pseudo-Class III relationship. "What I want you to know today": the skeletal Class I, II and III relationships, and pseudo-Class III from resorption. All of this affects where the teeth go, which he will teach in January.

Two more factors you can't get around. The tongue hypertrophies after the teeth are lost ("nature abhors a vacuum"): it fills the space where the teeth used to be, mostly a problem for the lower denture. And a recent extraction patient, with plenty of bone, is not easier: they are often harder, because a denture needs room for its base and teeth, and limited interarch space makes it much more difficult.

Support, stability and retention

The three most important things about any removable prosthesis. Asked on his specialty boards, he answered "without even firing up a neuron": support, stability and retention. "If there are three things I want you to remember off this slide."

ResistsWhat it means for the patient
SupportVertical force toward the tissues (closing and compressing the dentures)Some areas take it well: the buccal shelf and retromolar pad below, the palate above (the primary support areas); the ridges themselves aren't good at it
RetentionVertical dislodgement, away from the tissuesWhat patients focus on: peanut butter holds the dentures together as the jaw opens, the tongue lifts the lower denture. It bothers them, but it doesn't hurt
StabilityHorizontal force (sideways movement)The most important: a denture that slides sideways when they bite is extraordinarily painful, and they can't eat

"Of all the things that we need to address, stability is the most important." It is the one thing a dental implant is fabulous at: even two implants address stability, and that is life-changing for a patient who couldn't eat. Retention from implants is a plus. Humans are among the worst for stability: we don't chew like a shark, straight up and down; we move the jaw side to side. Denture occlusion, the shapes of the teeth as they fit together, contributes to all three, especially stability. The three are related: tipping is a horizontal movement, and it can also dislodge the denture, which is retention.

How the occlusion helps support, from the slides: the contacts must be bilateral, equal and simultaneous, on a well-fitting prosthesis. In centric occlusion both schemes direct the force toward the ridges, onto the primary support areas: non-balanced through a flat plane parallel to the denture base, balanced through cusp-to-fossa contact.

Centric relation and centric occlusion in a denture

When the muscles of a denture patient contract, they seat the joints, so centric relation is pretty easy to find (most patients don't posture forward, though some skeletal Class IIs will). Contact of the denture teeth with the joints seated is centric occlusion: the joints seated and the denture teeth fully interdigitated, as best they're designed to. MIP is not a term used for dentures: maximum intercuspation is a neuromuscular response, and there is no neuromuscular response with a denture.

In centric occlusion, the denture teeth contact usually only in the posterior. The anterior teeth are protected, because the bone at the front of the edentulous maxilla, the premaxilla, doesn't take forces well once the teeth are gone. All the occlusal function is generally on the posterior teeth; the anteriors are for appearance.

The occlusal schemes

To keep a denture stable there are two basic approaches, plus a middle ground:

1. Balanced occlusion. Bonwill's idea of 125 years ago: keep the denture teeth touching everywhere the patient moves, in centric occlusion and in every eccentric position. It is also called bilateral balance (almost redundant: if it isn't balanced on both sides it isn't balanced) or anatomic occlusion, a widely used term he dislikes, since there is nothing natural about it.

2. Non-balanced occlusion. Contact in centric occlusion, but the denture is designed so it can't contact anywhere else: flat teeth, a flat occlusal plane, and an articulator set to something completely unlike the patient. The condylar guidance is set to zero; the patient never has zero, so whatever condylar guidance they have separates the dentures as they move. There is no anterior contact. Not contacting is another way to keep a denture from tipping. The slides also call it neutrocentric occlusion.

3. Lingualized occlusion. A modification: a tooth with an elongated maxillary lingual cusp that fits against a flat plane or a wide fossa on the mandibular teeth, "a little bit like a mortar and pestle." It is hugely popular because it is much easier to arrange the teeth, it can be set balanced or non-balanced, and it is most likely the scheme you will use for many of your dentures.

"That's why I like making these tables for you, because this table will basically give you the one how-to of how all this fits together":

BalancedNon-balancedLingualized
In centric occlusionPosterior teeth contactPosterior teeth contactMaxillary lingual cusps contact the mandibular teeth
In eccentric positionsContact on both sides (working and non-working) and in protrusionNo contact in any eccentric positionBalanced: contact in eccentric movements too (left-right balance); non-balanced: none
Anterior contactAllowed in protrusion with anatomic teeth (the posteriors stay in contact); with semi-anatomic teeth only if the plane or curve compensatesNoneNo: difficult, though it can be compensated (in class: never, since it can't be kept from tipping front to back)
Posterior teethAnatomic (30-33°) or semi-anatomicFlat (0°)Semi-anatomic maxillary teeth with a long lingual cusp, against 0-12° mandibular teeth with a wide fossa
ArticulatorProgrammed to match the patient: semi-adjustable, facebow, protrusive recordCondylar guidance set to 0°As for the scheme chosen
Plane and compensating curveUsed to keep the teeth togetherFlat: no compensating curveFlat when non-balanced; a little plane and curve to balance

Both balanced and non-balanced work well, and patients accept both. They differ in esthetics, in stability, and in whether anterior contact can be allowed: protrude a denture with the front teeth touching and it is very easy to tip and dislodge.

Balanced occlusion

By definition, balanced occlusion is the bilateral, simultaneous contact of the anterior and posterior teeth in centric and eccentric positions. In a working movement there is contact on both the left and the right side; if contact were on one side only, the one-piece upper or lower denture would be destabilized and might tip out, and patients can't work with that.

Bilateral balance had been around a long time, but the person who made it easier was Rudolph Hanau, an engineer, not a dentist. He saw that you can't create the occlusion in the mouth, because the tissues keep moving: he named it the Realeff ("resiliency and like effect"). So the occlusion is built on an articulator. If you try to mark a denture occlusion in the mouth with articulating paper, the denture tips as it squeezes into the soft tissues, everything marks, and it gives you the wrong information; the denture course teaches the clinical remount instead. The slides add Hanau's own rules: his balanced occlusion used heavy contacts on the first molars to make up for the Realeff of the soft tissues and the joints, and the precise balance built on an articulator isn't present in the mouth, so it is refined through clinical remounts, never by adjusting the occlusion in the mouth.

Hanau also gave us the relationships among the five determinants of occlusion (Hanau's quint). Thielemann's articulation formula (the one the Review lecture spells Thielmann) shows them as proportions: balance = (condylar guidance × anterior guidance) / (cusp angle × compensating curve × plane of occlusion). It first said incisal guidance; later, anterior guidance. Early on, cusp angle and cusp height were used interchangeably; today cusp angle is the term for dentures and cusp height for the natural dentition. The determinants were first used for their original purpose, keeping denture teeth together. For example, if you increase the plane of occlusion, then to keep the teeth together you flatten the compensating curve or use a flatter tooth. For the dentate patient we take the same principles and turn them around to keep the teeth apart: the same tool, used differently.

The slides sort the factors. Fixed: the condylar guidance (the patient's joints; you cannot change it) and the plane of occlusion, aligned to the interpupillary line and Camper's (ala-tragus) plane, which affects esthetics. In class he said the plane can change only a little: there can't be a negative plane, where you see the posterior teeth before the anterior teeth ("an aesthetic crime"). Variable: the anterior guidance (possible with anatomic teeth steep enough, difficult with semi-anatomic teeth, and mostly unused, since the anterior teeth usually don't touch), the compensating curve and the cusp angle (the teeth chosen). So balance comes mainly from the compensating curve, the cusp angle and what little the plane of occlusion can change.

A balanced setup on an articulator: the sagittal condylar inclination is set from a protrusive record, the plane of occlusion by Camper's line and the interpupillary line, and a compensating curve is built in. In centric occlusion the teeth intercuspate; in a working movement there are contacts on both sides, and on the non-working side at the same time. It is not easy to set up; that technique is January's, and much of it will be digital in your future.

Non-balanced occlusion

Defined: flat (zero-degree) teeth set in an anteroposterior plane parallel to the denture foundation (the ridges), with no guidance and no compensating curve. Drawn, it looks a bit ugly, but it works. The slides call it the neutrocentric concept (citing Sears, 1949, and DeVan, 1954): neutralize the inclines and centralize the forces.

The thinking behind it: does bilateral balance even apply while chewing? With a bolus of food between the teeth, there is no balance at all, and the chance of tipping a denture is very significant. That is why denture patients are trained to put food on both sides of the mouth, chew as vertically as they can, avoid big bites (biting into a sandwich tips the back down and flips the lower denture up) and chew on the premolars rather than the incisors: "the incisors are for smiling, but the posterior teeth allow you to chew." Only as the food breaks down do the teeth come together. "Enter bolus, exit balance," as the slides quote it (from Prime, and from Boucher in 1961).

So the non-balanced idea: allow contact only on closure into centric occlusion, separate in every eccentric movement, and keep the forces centralized, never lateral or horizontal. The neutralizing factors are the cusp angle, the plane of occlusion, the compensating curve and the anterior guidance, all made flat, and the articulator's condylar guidance is artificially set to zero. The slides give five tooth factors. Position: as far lingual as the tongue allows. Proportion: the buccolingual width narrowed by 40% to decrease the stress on the ridge. Pitch: parallel to the planes of the denture bases, with no compensating curve and no anterior guidance (the patient is told not to incise in protrusion). Form: cuspless. Number: the mandibular second molars may be removed to keep the occlusion flat ahead of the ascending ramus, which starts to rise there. That makes it very easy to set up. The old flat teeth weren't esthetic, but they functioned well even for patients without good ridge height. Today's flat teeth have functionally flat surfaces that don't look flat, and with most of the esthetics coming from the anterior teeth, they look fine.

Lingualized occlusion

The middle ground. The slides define it: semi-anatomic maxillary teeth with an elongated palatal (lingual) cusp, against 0-12° mandibular teeth with a widened fossa, and no contact of the buccal cusps: a mortar-and-pestle contact that helps grind the food. Its early form simply tipped a 12° tooth against a 0° tooth, which opened the buccal space too much; today's teeth are made for it and look better, with the interdental spaces closed. Non-balanced lingualized: contact in centric occlusion only; the lingual cusps hit and there is no eccentric contact. Balanced lingualized: contact in centric occlusion and in eccentric movements, the lingual cusp sitting in the fossa, with a little plane of occlusion and compensating curve to give left-right balance. Anterior contact: in class he said never, because it can't be kept from tipping front to back; the slides' table says no, it is difficult, though it can be compensated. It is widely used in the school's clinic.

Which way to set it depends on what the patient brings. Non-balanced: a lot of ridge resorption, flabby tissues, poor oral awareness or dexterity, difficult jaw relations. Balanced: healthy, good ridges, firm mucosa, good awareness and good muscular dexterity. The slides list seven advantages: the centric contacts move half a tooth lingual, a more favorable lever; the force is centered over the ridge crest (slightly lingual in the molar area); there is only one contact point; minimal frictional contact; the maxillary buccal cusps are buccalized, leaving escape ways for food; working and balancing contacts are simpler, since only one cusp occludes; and it works with any ridge morphology, so with almost any patient, young to old. It is also easier to set. Disadvantage: with fewer teeth touching, wear shows sooner, and the patient may lose vertical dimension of occlusion (VDO).

The four schemes compared

The slides end the schemes with a summary table: subjective ratings, from − (a drawback) up to +++ (the strongest).

BalancedBalanced lingualizedNon-balanced lingualizedNon-balanced
Esthetics+++++−
Penetration of food+++−
Stability during function+++−−
Simpler technique−−+++
Less precise records−−+++
Decreased lateral forces−−+++
Ease of adjustment−++++++
Class II and III jaw relations−−++
Stability with centralized forces−−++

Read it as a trade: balanced wins on esthetics and on stability during function; the flatter and less balanced the scheme, the simpler it is to make, record and adjust, the less lateral force it puts on the ridges, and the better it suits Class II and III jaw relations.

Denture teeth: what they're made of

PorcelainComposite and cross-linked resinAcrylic
EstheticsVery esthetic, often the mostGood; layers improve translucencyFair; may stain
WearMinimal, so it maintains the vertical dimensionMulti-cross-linked for wear resistance, but it still wears: in 5-7 years the teeth are worn to a reverse curve and chew inefficientlyLess wear resistance
Bond to the denture baseNone: held mechanically, with pins (anterior teeth) or diatorics, holes with undercuts (posterior teeth)Chemical bondChemical bond to the acrylic base
HandlingMay chip or fracture; denser and harder than crown and bridge porcelain, so difficult to set and adjust; clicks against each otherDon't chip; softer sounds; easier to adjust and polish; expensiveLow cost; easy to shape and adjust; can be ground to fit a small interarch distance
Used forHigh-end denturesThe most common: most good dentures today, the number one go-toMainly temporary (interim) prostheses

Composite and cross-linked teeth come in many molds (one line on the slides offers up to 26 upper and 15 lower anterior molds and 8 posterior molds) and in shade systems such as Vita's: 16 shades in four groups, A to D, plus 2 bleach shades. When denture teeth wear, the patient closes farther, so wear can cost vertical dimension: you want the highest wear resistance you can get.

Choosing the teeth

Denture teeth come from manufacturers' mold charts (for example Dentsply's True Expression, or Ivoclar's BlueLine DCL, dual cross-linked, which the school uses most). The teeth are engineered in sets: a particular maxillary posterior tooth is meant to articulate with a particular mandibular posterior tooth, "just like a ball and socket."

You choose one maxillary anterior mold clinically (his example: A22). The chart gives its measurements (canine to canine, measured flat or on the curve of the arch, and the length of the central incisor) and its shape, then lists what is engineered to go with it: the mandibular anterior mold (A3) and the posterior molds for each occlusal scheme. In Ivoclar's language: orthoplane (flat, 0°, non-balanced), ortholingual (lingualized, balanced or non-balanced), orthotyp (semi-anatomic) and postaris (anatomic, for full bilateral balance). "The first take-home point about denture occlusion is that the denture occlusion is entirely based upon whatever selection we make to pick out that anterior maxillary mold." Everything else is engineered to follow it.

And the anterior mold is chosen more on esthetics than occlusion. Personality still shows up: every manufacturer's chart still has soft and bold molds (the temperamental theory, alive in 2026), and general shapes, square, tapering or ovoid (even combinations, "if you're the indecisive type").

Clinical guides: the wax rim on a record base, shaped in the mouth (January), shows the lip support, where the incisal edge goes (how far forward and how long the teeth should be), the midline and the canine positions, and its shape becomes the occlusal plane: the teeth are set to fit the wax rim. Berry's ratio (his biometric method, 1906): the central incisor about 1/16 of the bizygomatic width. "Do you think that's scientifically valid? And the answer is absolutely not. Does it tend to work for a lot of patients? ... Yeah, it actually does." The ala-to-ala width of the nose, with a gauge, suggests small, medium or large molds and correlates somewhat with canine position: not scientifically valid either, but a quick way to something that looks good. A recurring theme in tooth selection.

The posterior tooth form depends on the scheme you build: non-balanced needs flat teeth. Factors in choosing: the patient's neuromuscular control, the arch (ridge) morphology, the jaw relations (Class I, II, III), the interarch distance ("a big one"), the arch length, and whether they have worn dentures before: even experienced wearers start from ground zero with new dentures. Also shade: natural, fitted to the patient's complexion; the brightest and whitest can look fake ("you don't want headlights"). Denture teeth tend to be smaller than natural teeth, because they are easier to set. Larger arches need larger molds.

The slides give six criteria for the posterior teeth: the color, in harmony with the anterior teeth; a buccolingual width less than the natural teeth; an occlusogingival length set by the interarch distance and in harmony with the length of the canine; a mesiodistal length that fills the space from the distal of the canine to the retromolar pad; the cuspal inclination; and the material.

Tooth forms compared

AnatomicSemi-anatomicNon-anatomic (flat)
Cusp angle30-33° (the handout: 30° or more): sulci, ridges, look like teethLower, about 12-22° depending on the mold (the 12° and 20° molds); lingualized maxillary teeth belong here0°
SchemeBalanced; can let the anterior teeth touch in protrusionBalanced or not; lower lateral forces; can't support anterior contact unless the plane or curve compensatesNon-balanced
For itBest esthetics; chewing efficiency (controversial); resist rotation of the base; guide jaw closure into centric; less force per unit area on the ridges; the incisal guidance can be balancedEasier stability; can still be set in balanceLeast lateral force, so stability is easiest; any jaw relation (Class I, II, III) and crossbite; simpler to adjust; poor neuromuscular control; fewer complications
Against itNeeds a protrusive record and a facebow on a semi-adjustable articulator; more skill (a technician sets one in 20 minutes, your first takes days); hard to refine; more horizontal force through the cusps, so more bone deformation; short-lived results as the denture settles and inexpensive teeth wear; difficult with abnormal jaw relationsNot quite as estheticLess esthetic (old ones "dog-ugly"); poor penetration of food, so more pressure on the ridges and more lateral chewing; difficult to balance; a psychological drawback for some patients. Clinically acceptable

Other names, from the slides: semi-anatomic teeth are also called functional or anatoline teeth; non-anatomic teeth are also called cuspless, zero-degree, rational, flat-plane or monoline teeth.

Some claims have no support, he said: that cusps give the patient a "point of return" through neuromuscular feedback (there is none with a denture; the slides still list it among the advantages of cusps), or that a flat tooth is uncomfortable to close against.

What the evidence says

Balanced occlusion with good anatomic teeth gives the very best esthetics, but even today's non-balanced flat teeth look "pretty darn good," and esthetics has never held him back from a non-balanced occlusion when it was best for the patient. Anatomic teeth do penetrate and grind food better, but that isn't clinically significant: flat-plane, non-balanced dentures are clinically just as successful, and patients maintain great nutrition. "Both of them cross the finish line just fine." The ability to masticate is one factor of many in selecting teeth. Most patients simply want to smile at their grandchildren and eat a nice meal without embarrassment, and any of these schemes can get them there.

The slides cite a systematic review (Abduo, 2013, in the International Journal of Prosthodontics): anatomic teeth set in balanced or lingualized occlusion are preferable to flat teeth set non-balanced, mainly for patient acceptance. The literature is inconclusive but tends to favor cusps, and all the schemes are generally successful.

Looking ahead: partial dentures and implants

Not everybody loses all their teeth. For a partial denture it's simple: the more teeth that have been lost, the more you think like a denture, an occlusion that keeps the prosthesis stable, with support, stability and retention. The more natural teeth remain, the more you think like the dentate patient: canine guidance or group function, and posterior disclusion, because the teeth are in charge, not the prosthesis. With implants, more factors come in: what the opposing arch is, how many implants were placed, and the reminder that every removable prosthesis has some motion, such as rotation.

The mindset: denture occlusion is all about keeping the prosthesis in the mouth. The denture teeth are parts of an upper prosthesis and a lower prosthesis, each working as a single unit, so balance means resisting tipping, and stability is the property that matters most. Complete dentures start in January in the PCD course, with him.
full.nccl:
What's tested
  • Carious vs noncarious cervical lesions: the same place on the tooth, a different cause
  • The three causes of NCCLs, alone or together: abrasion (toothbrushing), abfraction (occlusion) and erosion (acid)
  • Abrasion: the toothpaste matters more than the toothbrush; relative dentin abrasivity (RDA); soft brushes, less pressure and the dominant-side clue
  • The evidence that not every NCCL comes from toothbrushing
  • Abfraction: why a load on an inclined plane makes a lesion at the cervical area (compression, tension and the fulcrum), its clues and the night guard
  • Erosion vs caries, where vomiting erodes and why, pH vs buffering capacity, and which drinks are worst
  • Matching the treatment to the cause, and when an NCCL needs a restoration

This lecture is Dr. Lawson's, prerecorded for the 11/12 session. He starts with a confession: as a dental student he wouldn't have known the difference between a noncarious cervical lesion (NCCL) and a carious cervical lesion. "I would have just said they're all class fives," without thinking hard about why a patient would need a filling down by the gum.

Carious or noncarious?

A lot of plaque can sit at the cervical area of a tooth, so caries-mediated lesions form there. They look like caries: soft and brown. They are difficult to restore, sitting under the gums in a patient at risk for caries, and a great option for them is resin-modified glass ionomer. Noncarious cervical lesions are in the same location but have a completely different etiology: they are caused by factors that are not caries.

NCCLs are multifactorial. There are three causes, and a lesion can come from one of them, two of them or all three:

CauseComes fromWhat to do about it
AbrasionToothbrushing, above all the toothpasteA lower-RDA toothpaste; if it's already low, less pressure, with an electric toothbrush that has a pressure sensor
AbfractionOcclusion: loads on the occlusal surface flex the toothA night guard (occlusal splint) to grind on instead of the teeth
ErosionAcid sitting on the teethA less acidic drink; bicarbonate to raise the mouth's pH; perhaps a water rinse

Abrasion: the toothbrush and the toothpaste

The evidence that brushing can do it. At a lecture he once heard a researcher, Dzakovich ("I can't pronounce his name"), take the position that all NCCLs are produced by toothbrushing. His study brushed extracted teeth set in artificial gums and recreated the look of an NCCL by brushing near the gum line. It also showed that commercial toothbrushes used without toothpaste did not create NCCLs: the toothpaste matters more than the toothbrush. So when you suspect a patient's lesions come from abrasion, talk with them about the toothpaste they use.

Relative dentin abrasivity (RDA) rates how abrasive a toothpaste is: the higher the number, the more abrasive, and the lower the number, the less. Recommend toothpastes with lower numbers. On his chart, a Colgate whitening toothpaste is about 124, and Crest Pro-Health is always very high. You used to have to look a toothpaste up on a list; now you can ask an AI chatbot, which (live in the recording) gave the same 124 as the chart.

The brush and how it's used. Most dentists recommend a soft-bristle toothbrush. The study made the toothpaste look more important than the brush, but soft brushes aren't only about abrasion lesions: they are also for gingival health. "Sometimes I forget that there's the pink parts of the mouth." Oral hygiene has to consider both caries and periodontal health. Technique matters too: tell the patient to brush with less pressure. Pressure is hard to judge, so an electric toothbrush with a pressure sensor helps the patient make sure they aren't pressing too hard (he uses one himself).

The dominant-side clue. People push harder on the side of their dominant hand, while on the other side they have to pull. So abrasion that looks worse on the patient's dominant side than on the other side points to the toothbrush. A patient with abrasion lesions on the left side but not the right? Ask, "Are you left-handed?" Those are the patients to coach on brushing more gently, perhaps with an electric toothbrush with a sensor.

Not every NCCL comes from toothbrushing

Some people say all NCCLs come from toothbrushing. That isn't true, and there is evidence against it:

  • Studies of populations with leprosy, people unable to brush their own teeth, found NCCLs.
  • Archaeological populations had NCCLs in times and places where toothbrushes hadn't been invented yet.
  • Animals get them: his mentor, Dr. Burgess, showed a camel with an NCCL, and a study shows NCCLs in a cat (they don't look quite like the ones in people).
  • NCCLs form where a toothbrush doesn't easily go: on the palate, where people don't usually brush, and even subgingivally, where the bristles can't reach.

So some NCCLs are caused by toothbrushing, and the rest need another cause.

Abfraction: the occlusion

How can a load on the occlusal surface make a lesion on the side of the tooth, at the cervical area? Studies show that loads on the inclined planes of the occlusal surface cause stress at the cervical part of the tooth. In materials science, things are almost always stronger in compression than in tension (being pulled apart). A load the tooth isn't supposed to have, on an inclined plane, pushes the crown to one side. The fulcrum is where the tooth is anchored in the bone.
