One side of the tooth is compressed; on the other side, tensile forces pull apart the bonds within the tooth structure, and where those tensile stresses are, abfraction lesions can form, just above the fulcrum.

His analogy: push on a stop sign. It is anchored in the ground (the fulcrum), the side being stretched is under tension, and that's where the damage can occur. In the tooth, the fulcrum is where it is anchored in the bone, and the NCCL forms just above it.

How would you know a lesion is abfraction and not abrasion? "It's hard to know," but look for clues that the patient loads their teeth heavily: exostoses and tori sometimes accompany NCCLs, along with opposing wear facets or other generalized wear that shows the patient is wearing their teeth.

What to do: an occlusal splint, a night guard (he apologizes in advance to Dr. Givan if that isn't the right term). This one isn't treating TMD: it is a piece of plastic between the patient's teeth, so they grind a sacrificial piece of plastic instead of their teeth. Any of these lesions can also be restored for esthetic reasons if needed.

Dr. Givan's L7 slides add a caution: abfraction is supported by in vitro studies, but clinical documentation has neither validated nor rejected it, so he doesn't count it as a primary mechanism of wear. Both lectures agree that NCCLs are multifactorial.

Erosion: acid that isn't caries

In a sense all destruction of teeth comes down to acid: a cavity is lactic acid dissolving enamel. But caries is bacteria-mediated demineralization, so it occurs only where plaque stagnates: the cervical areas of the teeth, around orthodontic brackets, the occlusal grooves, and proximally just below the contact point. Erosion happens wherever acidic fluids sit, and it isn't the same as caries.

Cupped-out cusp tips. Why do eroded molars show cupped-out areas where the cusp tips used to be? (A side point, he said, "not totally related to this lecture," but one he always thought was cool.) It's a combination of wear and erosion. The patient wears through the enamel of a cusp tip until a pinpoint of dentin shows: the dentin horn under each cusp. As soon as that dentin is exposed, acid selectively dissolves it, because dentin has a higher critical pH than enamel.

Vomiting (bulimia, or anyone who throws up a lot) erodes the lingual of the maxillary teeth, mostly the anterior teeth: the facial surfaces are protected by the lip, and the lingual of the mandibular teeth by the tongue. And when acidic fluids sit at the cervical area of the teeth, they make noncarious cervical lesions.

Talking to patients about what they drink

The first thing to do about erosion is to talk with patients about the acidic things they eat and drink. A dental school classmate of his measured the pH of a whole range of beverages and ranked them from the lowest pH (the worst) to higher. Don't assume patients know what pH numbers mean: plenty of very smart people don't. Give them reference points (he likens the most acidic end of the chart to battery acid; water is 7) and tell them how acidic some of their drinks are.

His chart covers more than soft drinks. Coffee: adding milk makes it less acidic (good news for his cappuccinos), and tea is better than coffee. Sparkling waters: what sets their acidity is the amount of carbonic acid, not the flavor, so the bubblier, more carbonated ones are more acidic.

pH vs buffering capacity

A newer idea is buffering capacity: how much bicarbonate, and so how much of your saliva, it takes to neutralize a drink. If a drink with a pH of 4 takes a lot of bicarbonate to neutralize, it has a high buffering capacity, and that's bad. If it takes only a little saliva, it has a low buffering capacity, and that's good: it is easier to neutralize after you eat or drink it.

pH and buffering capacity sound as if they should be the same thing, but they aren't, and they are measured differently. You measure pH by putting a pH probe in the solution. You measure buffering capacity by adding bicarbonate a little at a time and measuring how much it takes to bring the pH back to neutral.

A dental student in their lab (later a resident, now an endodontist) measured both for a whole range of beverages. Ranked by buffering capacity, the drinks stayed in about the same order as by pH, with two exceptions: orange juice and wine became "way, way bad." People drink orange juice all the time, so for a patient with a lot of erosion, ask about citrus drinks. Citric acid is a chelator: it wraps around calcium, so citrus drinks and citrus fruit can be extremely erosive to enamel.

Telling a patient with erosion to drink only water and milk may make them "lose the will to live," so give them something good that isn't bad for their teeth: Milo's sweet tea, and made with Splenda it has no fermentable sugar either.

Raising the pH

He measured the pH of many mouth rinses too ("kind of a waste of time"): some are low, but you rinse for about 30 seconds, maybe twice a day, so it's probably not a big deal.

For a patient with a lot of erosion, you can raise the mouth's pH with a base: bicarbonate. Basic Bites are candies that contain bicarbonate and arginine, a prebiotic, and they can help raise the pH of the mouth (he brought them up as an aside, and they are back in his summary). A patient can also rinse with baking soda, which is bicarbonate.

Some advice makes sense but, as far as he knows, has no evidence behind it ("kind of wives' tales"):

  • Keep acidic drinks to mealtimes (maybe the cheese on your hamburger helps neutralize your Coca-Cola).
  • Drink through a straw (he teases a colleague who sends his Diet Coke straight past his teeth).
  • Rinse with water after drinking soda or juice.

Why water may help less than he'd like: pH is on a logarithmic scale. In the lab, doubling an acid with water doesn't meaningfully change its pH; you'd need "a swimming pool of water." To neutralize an acid before pouring it down the sink, you add a base, such as bicarbonate. Water is fine, just probably not as effective as he wishes. Checking the mouth's pH with pH strips isn't easy either: his own saliva always reads about neutral.

Match the treatment to the cause

There is value in figuring out the etiology of an NCCL, because then you can treat the cause. If all of a patient's lesions come from sucking on lemons all day, there's little point in talking about the RDA of their toothpaste. To keep the lesions from getting bigger:

  • Toothbrushing: switch to a lower-RDA toothpaste. If it's already low, the patient may be pressing too hard: an electric toothbrush with a pressure sensor.
  • Acid: switch to a less acidic drink; rinse with water after meals (he doesn't know of evidence for it); bicarbonate, such as Basic Bites.
  • Abfraction: a night guard.

When to restore an NCCL

What he learned in dental school (not official, he says): you don't necessarily need to restore an NCCL if it is cleansable, doesn't hurt, doesn't look bad and isn't so deep that it is getting close to the pulp. A lesion that can't be cleaned, hurts, looks bad or is deep is the one to restore.

The same idea as Dr. Givan's L7 slides, which restore NCCLs only when it becomes necessary (progression, sensitivity, poor esthetics, food collection). Find the cause, treat it, and restore when a lesion is a problem.

plain.review:
What's tested
  • The basic words: occlusion, articulation, neutral zone, occlusal plane, the curves
  • MIP vs centric occlusion vs centric relation
  • Angle classes and "which cusp hits where"
  • Working, non-working and forward movements; canine guidance and group function
  • What makes back-tooth cusps taller or shorter; vertical dimension; the envelope of motion; articulator parts

This first lecture is a review of what you learned last spring, because everything else in occlusion builds on it. Dr. Givan also posted a help sheet called "What cusp hits where?", because those questions show up on every exam and on boards.

Basic words

Occlusion is how the upper and lower teeth touch when they are still. Articulation is how they touch both still and while the jaw moves. People mix them up, but they are not the same.

The neutral zone is the space where the push of the tongue from inside equals the push of the lips and cheeks from outside. Teeth grow into it, and anything you build outside it gets pushed around and tends to fail.

The occlusal plane is the average level of the biting surfaces. It is not really flat; it is an average of a curve. Seen from the side, the teeth follow the curve of Spee: from the lower canine tip, along the outer cusp tips of the back teeth, up to the front of the jaw joint. Seen from the front, they follow the curve of Wilson: cupped (concave) in the lower arch and domed (convex) in the upper, because upper back teeth tip outward and lower ones tip inward. For denture teeth, both curves together are called the compensating curve. The sphere of Monson is an old idea that all the cusps sit on a ball about 4 inches in radius, centered near the forehead between the eyebrows (glabella).

How the teeth fit

Normally the upper teeth's tongue-side cusps and the lower teeth's cheek-side cusps sit in the grooves down the middle of the opposite teeth. These are the centric (holding) cusps: wide and round, about a third of the tooth's width, and they hold up the height of your bite. The other cusps, the non-centric ones, are sharper and about a sixth of the width; they shear food, protect the cheek and tongue, and keep food on the chewing table. In a crossbite the arrangement is flipped. That's fine functionally, and implant crowns often have to be made that way.

The upper arch is a bit bigger than the lower (about 128 vs 126 mm long). The chewing table is about half to 60% of a back tooth's width. Contacts between teeth sit toward the cheek side, which makes the gaps on the tongue side bigger, so food falls back toward the tongue.

Three positions people confuse

MIP (maximum intercuspation) is simply where your teeth fit together best, no matter where the jaw joints are. Your nervous system finds it to protect your teeth, and it changes whenever teeth or fillings change.

Centric relation (CR) is a joint position: the jaw joints fully seated, up and forward against the bony bump in front of them (the articular eminence), on the thin middle part of each disc. It doesn't depend on the teeth, you can find it again and again, and from there the jaw can only hinge.

Centric occlusion (CO) is how the teeth touch when the joints are in CR. On Dr. Givan's tests, "centric occlusion" always means this, never MIP. In about 90% of people CO and MIP are different, by about 1.25 mm on average; a sideways difference is worse. The CO contact is often unstable, and closing into it (often at night) causes worn spots, cracked cusps and loose teeth. Teeth only touch about 18 minutes a day; the rest of the time the muscles keep the joints seated.

Angle classes

Class I (about 70%): normal molar fit. "Class I malocclusion" means the molars fit but other teeth are crowded or turned. Class II (about 25%): the lower first molar sits behind the upper. Division 1 has a narrow upper arch and front teeth sticking out; division 2 has a square arch, upper centrals tipped back, laterals flared and a deep bite (hard to restore). Class III (about 5%): the lower first molar sits in front; front teeth are edge to edge or the lower ones are in front. The old Class IV (one side each way) isn't used. If a test question doesn't say the class, assume Class I.

Most adults have cusp-to-marginal-ridge contacts (one tooth touching two). The textbook ideal, cusp-to-fossa (one tooth to one tooth), is rare in nature.

Which cusp hits where

Unless told otherwise, assume Class I and cusp-to-fossa. Draw "fence posts": a row for the upper teeth (canine, two premolars, then front and back halves of each molar) and a row for the lower, with each lower post a half step in front of its upper partner. Class II moves the lower row back a step; Class III moves it forward. The fence tells you which cusp is closest; your tooth anatomy tells you which fossa. For premolars in Class I and III, contacts land in the front (mesial) pits of the upper premolars and the back (distal) pits of the lower ones; Class II is the reverse. Example: in Class I the cheek cusp of #29 sits in the front pit of #4.

Front teeth

Vertical overlap (overbite) of 3-5 mm is normal, 3 mm is ideal; orthodontists accept about 1 mm to fit braces. Horizontal overlap is "overjet." An open bite is properly an "anterior open occlusal relationship." The shape of the back (tongue) side of the upper front teeth mostly decides the anterior guidance.

Moving the jaw

The jaw joint hinges and slides, and both sides are one bone, so it is very complicated. Any movement away from the fitted-together position is "eccentric." Moving forward, the joint slides down the bony slope and the back teeth separate (Christensen's phenomenon). If back teeth do hit, the lower teeth's front slopes meet the upper teeth's back slopes. Moving sideways, the side you move toward is the working side (its joint mostly spins); the other side is the non-working or "balancing" side (its joint swings forward and in). Contacts on the non-working side are interferences.

To figure out which slopes touch, draw the molars fitted together and move the lower tooth in your head. On the non-working side, the inner slopes of the two holding cusps meet. On the working side, the lower tongue-side cusp meets the upper tongue-side cusp, and the lower cheek-side cusp meets the upper cheek-side cusp. Paths across an upper tooth: forward is toward the front, working is toward the cheek, non-working is toward the front and palate. On a lower tooth they reverse: forward shows up as backward, working toward the tongue, non-working toward the back and cheek. In pictures, the starting contact is at the base of the arrow.

Guidance and the ideal

Canine guidance: the canines lift the back teeth apart when you move sideways. Group function: a few teeth share the job, useful when the canine is weak, missing or an implant. The guide closest to the teeth has the most effect, so the front teeth matter more than the joints. The ideal: all teeth touching evenly at once, forces straight down the roots, no non-working contacts, and canines or front teeth separating the back teeth. That is mutually protected occlusion: back teeth protect the front teeth when you bite, and front teeth protect the back teeth when you move.

How tall can back cusps be?

Things that separate the back teeth more allow taller cusps: a steeper joint slope or more vertical overlap. Things that separate them less need shorter cusps: more horizontal overlap, a bite plane that runs parallel to the joint path, a sharper curve of Spee, or more sideways shift of the jaw. For groove direction, everything widens the angle between the sideways paths except a wider distance between the two joints, which narrows it.

Bite height

VDO is face height with the teeth together. VDR is face height with the jaw resting. The difference, the freeway space, is usually 2-6 mm. Losing back teeth lets the bite collapse (posterior overclosure).

The envelope of motion

From CR the jaw can hinge open about 20-25 mm; to open wider (40-60 mm), the joints must slide forward. The outer limits of movement are "borders"; teeth limit the top border, and ligaments and joints limit the rest. Posselt drew these limits from the side, from above and from the front, and you should be able to name each line. We almost never use the borders except the top one; chewing happens in a small teardrop shape. The postural position is about 2-4 mm below MIP, held up by a reflex. It is not the same as the position of least muscle activity (about 8 mm down). Head position changes how the teeth meet: sitting up moves contacts forward compared with lying back, so always check fillings with the patient sitting up. The jaw can also shift sideways a little (Bennett movement), measured in millimeters or as an angle.

Articulators

An articulator is a machine that mimics the jaws and joints. It only helps if it is about the patient's size. Know the parts: upper and lower members, the anterior guide pin and table, mounting plates, condylar elements and the centric latch.

Occlusion works in microns: you can feel a hair between your teeth.
plain.anatomy:
What's tested
  • The hinge-and-slide joint, its disc and its two spaces
  • Which ligament stops which movement
  • Each chewing muscle, its parts and its job
  • The exam chart of muscles for each jaw movement
  • The muscles above and below the hyoid bone

This lecture is anatomy for dentists: how the jaw parts work, not every bump on the bone. Dr. Givan won't ask about nerves or blood supply.

The jaw joint

Dogs hinge, cows grind, and we do both. The jaw joint hinges like an elbow and slides like a wrist, so it's called ginglymoarthrodial. Both joints belong to one bone, so one side can't move without the other.

A pad called the disc sits between the jaw's knob (the condyle) and the skull. It is tough fibrous tissue that acts like an extra bone. Its middle is thin and has no blood vessels or nerves, and that's where the condyle normally sits; the front edge is thicker and the back edge thickest. It is also thicker toward the inside, so if it slips off, it tends to go forward or inward. Don't call it a meniscus; that's the crescent-shaped pad in the knee.

The disc splits the joint into two spaces. The jaw hinges in the lower space (condyle against disc) and slides in the upper space (disc against skull), so the disc always stays on top of the condyle. Behind the disc is tissue full of blood vessels and nerves; pressing on it hurts. Its upper layer is stretchy and pulls the disc back. The upper part of the lateral pterygoid muscle attaches to the front of the disc. The joint carries real force: you push against it every time you bite something hard.

Ligaments stop movement

The capsule wraps the joint and keeps the condyle from dropping out. Two small ligaments tie the disc to the inner and outer sides of the condyle; when they stretch or tear, the joint clicks (about half of people click, and ligaments don't heal). The stylomandibular and sphenomandibular ligaments limit opening and moving forward. The temporomandibular ligament has an outer slanted part that limits how far you can hinge open, and an inner flat part that stops the jaw being pushed back (like from a punch to the chin). If a patient can't close after a long appointment because the condyle slid past the bump, press down on the back of the lower jaw, never back.

How muscles work

Muscles can only pull. They always work in pairs, one pulling while its partner controls the motion. Parts of one muscle can fire separately, so one muscle can do several jobs. A muscle's shape and direction tell you its job.

The four chewing muscles

The masseter runs from the cheekbone to the angle of the jaw. It is the main power closer. Its outer part closes and pushes slightly forward; its deep part closes and pulls back. Because it pulls up and forward, it seats the joints.

The temporalis fans from the side of the head to the thin coronoid process. It is mostly a fast positioner, not a power closer. Its front fibers close, middle fibers close and pull back a bit, and back fibers pull the jaw back. The cheekbone arch protects where it attaches.

The lateral pterygoid is really two muscles. The lower part pulls the condyle forward, down and inward: both sides together push the jaw forward and help open; one side alone swings the chin to the other side. The upper part works when you close, holding the disc in place.

The medial pterygoid runs inside the jaw angle and closes the jaw. With the masseter outside, it forms a strong sling.

The exam chart

Dr. Givan will use this chart for "which muscle does which movement": closing: temporalis, masseter, medial pterygoid. Opening: the lower lateral pterygoid plus the muscles above and below the hyoid. Forward: the lower lateral pterygoid plus the outer masseter. Back: the back of the temporalis plus the deep masseter. To the right: the right temporalis and right masseter, plus the left lateral and left medial pterygoids (to the left, swap sides).

Opening and the hyoid

The hyoid is a floating bone in the neck that touches no other bone. Muscles above it (digastric, geniohyoid, mylohyoid, stylohyoid) help open the jaw. Muscles below it (sternohyoid, omohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid) hold the hyoid still so the upper group has something to pull against. The digastric is a key opener; the mylohyoid is the floor of the mouth. The big neck muscles (sternocleidomastoid and trapezius) hold the head up.
plain.function:
What's tested
  • The main jobs of the mouth and how the brain runs chewing
  • The chewing stroke and its numbers
  • What changes chewing, and bite force
  • Swallowing: types, numbers and the three stages
  • Speech: no tooth contact, "f" and "v," and "s"

When the teeth aren't touching, muscles and ligaments decide where the jaw is. The mouth's three main jobs are chewing, swallowing and speaking; breathing and showing emotion are secondary.

Chewing

Chewing is a steady rhythm of opening and closing, and it's the first step of digestion. Sensors in the gums and ligaments around the teeth, the tongue, the joints and the muscles report to the brainstem, which fires some muscles and quiets others. A "pattern generator" in the brainstem stores learned patterns (engrams), so chewing runs mostly on autopilot, like walking. If you bite something hard by surprise, a reflex stops the closing muscles and opens the jaw at once.

Each stroke opens mostly straight down, swings to the side at the bottom, then closes at an angle to crush the food and finishes with a small sideways grinding slide. A chewing stroke opens only about 16-18 mm and moves about 5-6 mm sideways. On the food side the jaw opens forward and comes back as it closes. Early in a bite there is more forward and sideways movement; it gets smaller as the food breaks down. Harder food means more sideways movement.

About 78% of people chew mostly on one side, usually the side with the best contacts. Teeth do touch while chewing, more often as the food gets softer, almost every stroke before swallowing, for about 0.2 seconds each, and they always come back to MIP ("home plate"). Tall cusps make an up-and-down stroke; flat or worn cusps make a wider one. Someone who grinds flat has no single MIP, just a zone. People with jaw pain chew slower, shorter and less evenly.

Bite force: the strongest ever measured was 975 lb; men are about 118-142 lb, women about 79-99 lb. Back molars bite three to five times harder than front teeth, which is why front teeth can handle angled forces. Long-faced people bite softer; square-faced people bite harder. A filling left half a millimeter high doubles the force on that tooth. Most serious chewing happens at the second premolar and first molar. Dentures give only a fraction of normal force. The tongue is the mouth's knife, fork and spoon, and the cheek muscle (buccinator) works with it.

Swallowing

Swallowing (deglutition) moves food from the mouth to the stomach, mostly by reflex. You decide to swallow based on how fine the food is, how much taste you've gotten out of it, and how wet it is. Adults steady the jaw by putting the teeth together in MIP (a somatic swallow). Babies, without teeth, push the tongue forward between the gums (a visceral swallow). Keeping that baby swallow too long pushes the front teeth forward and can cause an open bite. A swallow presses the teeth harder (about 66 lb) and longer than chewing. We swallow about 590 times a day.

There are three stages. First, the tongue presses the food against the roof of the mouth with the lips closed and teeth together, and pushes it back. Second, throat muscles squeeze it down, the soft palate closes off the nose, the epiglottis covers the windpipe, and the ear tubes open; the first two stages take about a second. Third, the esophagus carries it to the stomach in about 6-7 seconds.

Speech

Air from the lungs passes the vocal cords, which make the pitch; the tongue, lips, cheeks and jaw shape the sound. Speech is a learned reflex, and the teeth do not touch while talking. For "f" and "v," the upper front teeth should just touch the line where the wet and dry parts of the lower lip meet; if they press into the lip they're too long, and if the sound is hard to make they may be too short. For "s," the teeth come closest (about 1-2 mm), which dentists use to judge bite height. For "m," the lips close and air goes out the nose.
plain.concepts:
What's tested
  • Who came up with which idea
  • The two old schools and what they learned
  • Today's competing ideas and what they agree on
  • The four modern rules: back-teeth support first, a good bite plane, the right kind of contacts, and front-teeth guidance
  • Dawson's smile-design steps and speech checks

Real patients rarely look like the perfect model, but the same principles still apply. They came from about 175 years of ideas, first for dentures and later for natural teeth.

History

Bonwill, the "father of articulation," found that the two jaw joints and the chin make a triangle with sides about 4 inches. That led to the idea of a bite plane and to balanced dentures, where teeth touch everywhere so the denture doesn't tip. Balkwill saw the moving joint shift inward during sideways movement; von Spee described the side-view curve; Christensen saw the back teeth separate when the jaw moves forward and made a record of it; Parfitt first put curved joint paths on an articulator; Bennett described the jaw's sideways shift. Monson combined these into the idea that the teeth sit on a 4-inch ball; his articulator spun around a center point instead of copying the joints.

Two schools

Pankey, Mann and Schuyler built the lower back teeth to Monson's curve, then shaped the upper back teeth from paths the patient ground into wax. They didn't think an articulator needed to copy the joints. Schuyler later dropped the balancing contacts, made the front-teeth guidance more important, and used simpler tools.

Gnathology tried to copy the patient exactly: find the joints' hinge centers, trace every movement, and set a fully adjustable articulator. Early on it pushed the jaw all the way back (rearmost, uppermost, midmost) and used balanced contacts, both mistakes. Gnathologists later gave us canine guidance (Stallard and Stuart; keyword: separation) and mutually protected occlusion (D'Amico; keyword: force), plus P.K. Thomas's waxing. Digital jaw tracking has brought the "copy the patient" goal back.

Today's ideas

Conformative: keep what the patient has (most everyday dentistry, if things are healthy). Gnathology: copy the joints' movement. Pankey/Dawson: respect the seated joint and focus on front-teeth guidance. Bioesthetics: good looks and good function go together; bite height set from a fixed measurement; strong front overlap. Neuromuscular: build the bite where muscles are most relaxed, found with an electrical stimulator; this usually means raising the bite and redoing every tooth, and it puts the jaw too far forward, so UAB doesn't teach it. All of them agree that all teeth should touch at once and back teeth shouldn't bump when the jaw moves. Speer's test for any idea: does it work for every patient, and can you do it without drilling teeth?

Four rules

1. Back-tooth support comes first. Without back teeth, the front teeth take all the force and break down, and the bite collapses. Fixing only the six front teeth a patient wants won't last. You don't need every molar: teeth back to the second premolar (a "shortened dental arch") work fine.

2. Fix the bite plane. Teeth that drift or over-erupt get in the way of every movement. Small problems can be smoothed (enameloplasty), bigger ones crowned, and severe ones may need the tooth removed.

3. Use the right contacts. The old "tripod" contact (each cusp touching three spots) is very stable but hard to make, especially in porcelain, and needs the teeth to separate right away. Today we use point to flat surface: forces go straight down the root and there's a little "freedom" to slide, side to side for the jaw's sideways shift, and front to back for a small slide (a "long centric").

4. Front-teeth guidance matters most. The back (tongue) side of the upper front teeth must fit the paths the jaw actually uses. To rebuild it: wax it up, try it in temporaries, record the paths on a custom guide table, and copy them in the final crowns.

Dawson's smile design

In order: set the holding contacts; check lip support (a bulge at the gumline usually means the tooth wasn't trimmed enough); make sure the lips close easily; check "f" and "v" against the lower lip and the smile line; shape the tongue side for smooth guidance; round the bump near the gum (cingulum) for "d" and "t" (too bulky can push teeth forward in a tongue-thruster); and check "s": too much space causes a lisp, too little a whistle.
plain.applying:
What's tested
  • When to copy the existing bite
  • What to check in sideways and forward movements
  • Keeping the bite vs rebuilding it, and how to take bite records
  • Rules for each kind of filling, crown and bridge
  • Implants: why and how their bite is different

This is where occlusion meets everyday restorative work. Patients often have problems (worn spots, cracks, loose teeth) before they have symptoms, and replacing a broken crown doesn't fix the force that broke it.

Guidance and MIP

Accepted bite schemes are balanced (for dentures), mutually protected, and group function. If a patient has no problems, copy the guidance they already have. MIP is where chewing ends and where you swallow, but it isn't stable long-term. Teeth touch in MIP only about 17.5 minutes a day (about 1,800 chewing strokes and 500 swallows). The ligaments around the teeth can feel something 20 microns thick.

Check sideways movements for loose guiding teeth and smooth motion; a contact on the non-working side tends to steer the jaw. A patient who has lived with one for years can keep it, but don't create one. Check forward movement too: any back-tooth bumping in forward movement must be fixed before you restore the front teeth.

Keep the bite or rebuild it?

The conformative approach fits the new work into the existing bite, with only small local fixes (shortening a cusp that sticks down, removing a non-working contact or a deflecting spot). Use an MIP bite record. The reorganized approach rebuilds the whole bite starting from the seated joints (a CR record, taken by guiding the jaw with both hands), so you have a repeatable starting point, an even bite, and no new problems. To decide, compare where the teeth touch with the joints seated against MIP, and look for wear, cracks and loose teeth.

Bite-record materials include PVS (Regisil), wax (Aluwax), zinc oxide eugenol paste, acrylic and plaster. Wax sets in a second or two; PVS takes 20-30 seconds while the patient moves. Don't put material across the whole arch, and trim it so you can check the casts sit right. For an MIP record, put material only where the teeth don't touch, trim it to the cusp tips, and keep it off the gums. With rubbery materials, keep the patient biting while it sets, trim with a scalpel, and press the models together while mounting.

Back teeth

Every filling should touch the opposite tooth evenly, at the same time as the other teeth. It should not be high, should not push the tooth sideways, should not be left out of contact (the teeth drift into it, never in a good way), and should not touch on sideways movements. For a big filling, first check the opposite tooth for over-eruption and fix it. Several large back fillings may need a full rebuild with strong materials. A single crown between other teeth is usually conformative, best recorded by just fitting the models together by hand, with no face-bow and a simple articulator; at try-in check that it's fully seated and the side contacts are right before checking the bite. A crown at the end of the row needs a bite record so the model doesn't tip. Three-unit bridges are usually conformative, with a good opposite bite plane and a semi-adjustable articulator. Whole quadrants may need the opposite side fixed first. A tiny hinge articulator only helps the lab, not you.

Front teeth

Small front fillings (Class III) copy the old contacts and keep the bite off the filling. Corner fillings (Class IV) should share contacts between filling and tooth. For one front crown, first fix any back-tooth bump that slides the jaw forward. When crowning both upper centrals or a canine, use a custom guide table; to copy the existing guidance, take its impression before trimming the teeth. If the guidance is poor, wax it up, wear temporaries for at least three weeks (months for grinders), record them, and copy them. Use "s" to check bite height: the front teeth should come within 1-2 mm.

Implants

An implant is fused to bone with no cushioning ligament, so it barely moves (2-3 microns down vs about 28 for a tooth). Its bite is built light: on a gentle close it barely touches, and on a hard clench it touches equally with the teeth, which sink a little. A front implant shouldn't do the canine guiding alone; it shares the load with natural teeth. A back implant should avoid contact in sideways and forward movements. Shimstock (a 12-micron strip) helps you check this.
plain.instruments:
What's tested
  • Why we mount models on an articulator
  • The three kinds of articulator and what each can and can't do
  • The facebow and the bite records: what each one is for and the mistakes that ruin a mounting
  • Why a forward (protrusive) record is preferred, and why records are taken 3-5 mm out
  • How to choose an articulator for a patient

This opens the second half of the course. An articulator is a hinge that holds the upper and lower models so you can study the bite and build restorations outside the mouth. Dr. Givan sorts them into three kinds: ones you can't adjust, ones you can partly adjust, and ones you set up completely for the patient. The machine is only a tool. His one line to remember: an articulator works best when it is about the size of the patient.

Why mount models

Mounted models let you see how the teeth fit, still and moving, from any angle. They show harmful contacts the patient avoids by reflex, so you can't see them in the mouth. For diagnosis, a CR mounting (jaw joints seated) is the most useful: you can see the first contact with the joints seated, the slide, and still close into MIP. An MIP mounting can't go back to the seated-joint contact.

Models also help plan treatment (try a grinding plan on the models first), make a diagnostic wax-up to see the end result and explain it to the patient, and most commonly build the restoration itself. The big point: the articulator you pick decides how long you spend adjusting the work at delivery. Time saved outside the appointment is money well spent.

Kinds of articulators

An arcon articulator (ARticulating CONdyle) has the condyle part on the lower member and the socket part on the upper member, like a real jaw. A non-arcon is the reverse and is usually cheaper. UAB groups articulators as non-adjustable (a hinge or average values), semi-adjustable (some settings, some averages, like your Denar 320) and fully adjustable (everything set for the patient). Real articulators sit on a sliding scale. Digital (virtual) articulators are close but still can't place the models relative to the patient's joints as well as a facebow does.

Non-adjustable

These are only accurate in one position: the teeth fully closed together (MIP). Their opening and side-to-side paths don't match the patient. Any bite record that props the teeth apart adds error, because the hinge closes along a different arc than the jaw, and the smaller the articulator, the bigger the error. They're cheap, quick and small, which helps the lab, not the dentist: the crown won't match the patient's movements, so you grind it in the mouth, losing its shape (and zirconia is hard to adjust and polish). Small partial-arch ones also can't show the other side. One that is about the size of a person, with the condyles about 4 inches apart, does a decent job.

Without a facebow, you can use a mounting stand on an articulator about 110 mm (4 inches) wide: center the upper model on the stand, plaster it to the upper arm, relate the lower model (with a bite record only if needed), and plaster it to the lower arm. That puts the models in an average position where average settings work.

Semi-adjustable

These can be set to move much like the patient, so both closing and side-to-side movements come out nearly right, from a single crown to a full-mouth rebuild. The two common settings:

1. Condylar guidance (sagittal condylar inclination): how steeply the condyle slides down the bump in front of the socket. It decides how much the back teeth separate when there's little front-tooth guidance, and how tall the cusps and how deep the grooves can be. One forward bite record sets both sides, or you pick a number: 20-30° is common for crowns, about 0° for one kind of flat denture.

2. Bennett angle: how far the condyle on the other side swings inward during a side move. It changes how wide the grooves in the back teeth are. It's adjusted less often; Dr. Givan would leave this one off first.

To use these settings you need information from the patient: a facebow for the upper model, and bite records for the lower model and the settings.

The facebow

The facebow places the upper model on the articulator in the same position it has relative to the patient's jaw joints. It uses three points: the two ear canals (close to the jaw's hinge) and one point in front (for your facebow, a mark 43 mm above the upper right lateral incisor's edge). The front point and a bubble level also capture the smile line and the tilt of the bite. It takes a minute or so. Ours is an arbitrary facebow: it guesses the hinge within about 2-5 mm, which is fine for nearly every patient. A kinematic facebow finds the exact hinge.

Skip the facebow and the upper model sits wrong: the smile line can come out tilted (a cant), the back teeth may hit in side and forward movements, the cusps can be the wrong height, and you grind more in the mouth. A model mounted too far back or too high makes the front-most teeth hit first or hard; too far forward or too low makes the back-most teeth hit.

Bite records

A CR record is taken with the joints seated and the teeth not touching (touching makes the jaw slide toward MIP), opened as little as possible, or at the height you plan to restore. Wax is often best: it sets in a second with air and water and the cusp tips seat in it well, but it's fragile. Use CR for diagnosis, full rebuilds and changes in bite height. In about 90% of people the seated-joint contact (CO) isn't the same as MIP.

The MIP record is the most common record and the most misused. Bad mounting is the second most common cause of lab problems, after bad impressions. If the models fit together by hand, don't use a record at all, because the lab will use whatever you send. If you need one: rubbery bite material (VPS) records more detail than stone and is springy, so it rarely fits the models unless trimmed; it takes 30-60 seconds to work and about 1.5 minutes before it can come out, and any movement distorts it. Don't cover the biting surfaces of teeth that aren't being prepared, keep it off the gums, and use a record base if too many teeth are missing. Wax sets instantly and needs little trimming, but needs a water bath and breaks easily.

Five rules for any bite record: it doesn't move teeth or squash the gums; you can check it in the mouth; it fits the models as well as the mouth; you can check it on the models; it doesn't distort on the way to the lab.

Forward and side records

These set up the articulator's movements. A forward (protrusive) record is taken with the jaw pushed straight forward 3-5 mm and sets the condylar guidance on both sides at once. Side (lateral) records need two, one each way, and each sets the opposite side's guidance and Bennett settings. Forward records are preferred: side records give a steeper angle, and if the articulator is steeper than the patient, the crown may hit in the mouth; if it's flatter, the back teeth just separate more. That's also why many people simply set 30°. Records are taken 3-5 mm out because the condyle's path curves; a record taken farther out gives a smaller Bennett angle and narrower grooves that are more likely to hit.

Calibrated articulators like the Denar 320 are interchangeable: the mounted models move between articulators (yours and the lab's) without losing accuracy.

Fully adjustable

These can copy almost everything: curved condyle paths, the side shift, the small wobble of the working-side condyle, and the distance between the condyles. Setting one up used to mean finding the exact hinge (once marked with a tattoo), then tracing jaw movements with a pantograph (six styluses drawing on six tables while a central pin keeps the teeth apart), which took hours. Today camera and scanner systems record jaw movements in minutes and feed digital articulators. Because the hinge is exact, the thickness of a CR record doesn't matter there. On a semi-adjustable one it does: keep CR records thin, or take them at the height you plan to restore.

Choosing one

Four things decide: the patient's bite (strong front-tooth guidance lets a simple articulator work for a back crown; weak guidance, as in edge-to-edge bites or very little overlap of the front teeth, needs a better one, and never use a non-adjustable for teeth that are part of the guidance), how much work you're doing (the job picks the tool), what the articulator can do, and the skill of the clinician: a semi-adjustable articulator in knowledgeable hands beats a fully adjustable one in inexperienced hands.
plain.malocclusion:
What's tested
  • How a "functional disturbance" happens: normal function plus an event that's more than you can tolerate gives symptoms
  • What a TMD is, and why it isn't one thing
  • The five causes: how the jaw and teeth fit, trauma, stress, deep pain and habits like grinding
  • What the evidence says about bite problems and TMD, and why grinding teeth "just in case" isn't done
  • Treatments: reversible first (splints), irreversible only when the bite is the cause
  • Loose teeth and worn teeth: what's normal, what isn't, and the kinds of wear
  • Grinding at night: it starts in the brain, not the bite, and a splint protects the teeth

This lecture (10/29) switches direction: instead of how occlusion works, it's about when things go wrong, why, and what we do. It sets up the TMD course in third year. Sometimes the bite has nothing to do with the problem; other times, working on the bite still helps the patient get better. Dr. Givan said to learn the general themes here; the details of each jaw disorder come next year.

Normal function and dysfunction

The jaw's normal jobs are chewing, swallowing and speaking. Dysfunction means those jobs are changed or blocked: you can't move the way you should, or it hurts. The cause of dysfunction is called a functional disturbance, and often we never find out why it started.

Examples: muscle problems (you can't open as wide; the bite suddenly feels "off" because a muscle's resting length changed), joint changes (the jaw swings to one side as it opens), too much force on the teeth (broken teeth, tooth pain, bone loss, wear), and headaches (there are over 250 kinds).

What a TMD is

People say "I have TMJ," but TMJ is the joint. The problem is a temporomandibular disorder, or TMD: an umbrella word for many different problems of the chewing muscles, the jaw joint, or both. Most change how the jaw works, and some hurt. About half are in the muscles, about a third in the joints, and the rest elsewhere, often mixed. There are more than 40 of them, each diagnosed and treated differently, so "I'm being treated for TMD" tells you almost nothing. The slides use Bell's classification. Many TMDs have nothing to do with the bite. A TMD is also not the same as orofacial pain, which is a much bigger group of head and neck pains.

Dentists have long blamed the bite for TMD. Today Dr. Givan says it differently: bite treatments can create an environment for healing, which helps, but that doesn't mean the bite caused the problem.

How a problem starts

The model is: normal function + an event, more than your tolerance → symptoms.

Normal function is run by the brainstem (learned patterns), adjusted by feedback from the mouth and by the emotional brain. An event can be local, like a high crown, a burn from hot pizza, a strain, grinding or ongoing pain, or body-wide, like stress or illness. Your tolerance depends on local things (how your bite places your jaw, and whether the joints sit stably) and body-wide things (genes, gender, diet, disease).

If the total stays under your tolerance, you adapt and feel nothing. If it goes over, symptoms start. Any part can change, so something you handled fine yesterday may be too much today. That's the typical TMD story: fine for years, then one Tuesday, terrible pain.

When the system breaks down you can see: tooth pain (pulpitis), worn or broken teeth, loose teeth, sore chewing muscles, jaw joint pain, ear pain and headaches.

The five causes

1. How the jaw and teeth fit (mandibular stability), 2. trauma, 3. emotional stress, 4. deep pain, 5. habits like clenching and grinding (parafunction). He spent the most time on the first, because it's the one dentists control.

1. How well the jaw and teeth fit

Mandibular stability means the teeth and both joints fit against the skull at the same time. The research linking bite and TMD is weak, partly because studies rarely say which TMD they looked at.

Pullinger and Seligman found these more often in TMD patients: a skeletal open bite in front, a slide of more than 2 mm from the first contact (joints seated) into the full bite, more than 4 mm of overjet, and five or more missing back teeth. But people without TMD have them too, so they concluded the bite isn't the most important factor. In a review of 57 studies, 22 found no link and 35 found some link, and a link doesn't prove cause.

Still, everyone agrees a good bite is the base of good dentistry: all teeth touching evenly at once, forces straight down the teeth, front teeth separating the back teeth when you move. Ideally the joints are fully seated (orthopedic stability) and the teeth fully together (occlusal stability). The five treatment goals: joints up and forward against the slope, discs in place between joint and socket, back teeth touching evenly with forces down the long axis, front teeth separating the back teeth in movements, and in the head-forward eating posture, slightly heavier back contacts than front.

The catch: only about 10% of people can close with their joints seated straight into their best bite. For everyone else, getting the teeth together pulls one or both joints off their seat. That's orthopedic instability, and it can lead to a problem inside the joint (an intracapsular disorder). The risk goes up with the size of the gap (1-2 mm usually isn't a problem; more than 3 mm raises the risk) and with heavy force, as in people who grind. Open bites and Class II bites have been linked to TMD, but not strongly.

His example: a patient in severe pain who had had lots of crowns and bridges over the years. Each one fit her teeth but pulled her jaw a little farther from its seated position, until one day she couldn't tolerate it. A full-coverage splint let her joints settle back, which opened a gap between her front teeth. She was rebuilt at that new position, in temporaries for over a year, about two years in all, and her pain was relieved. In her case the bite really was the problem.

2. The bite and the muscles

Bite something hard by surprise and your jaw pops open: a fast, automatic protective reflex in the brainstem. Studies of muscle activity showed that when back teeth don't touch, the closing muscles relax, and when the back molars touch, the muscles fire fully. So back-tooth contact turns the closing muscles on. Removing non-working side contacts keeps the masseter and temporalis quiet in that movement, which is one argument for canine guidance.

Normal function (ortho-function) uses this feedback. Parafunction (clenching, grinding, habits) doesn't: the muscles fight each other, tighten up and get tired and strained, and tooth contacts don't start it.

The high crown. Leave a new crown slightly high and the patient starts guarding: moving the jaw stiffly to avoid hitting it. That's protective co-contraction. It's a normal response, not a disease, but moving that way makes the muscles sore. Here the bite did cause a muscle problem.

But bite "interferences" a patient already has (non-working or working side contacts on back teeth) show up just as often in people with no symptoms. A slide under 2 mm is equally common in both groups; over 2 mm is more common in patients with symptoms. So: adding an interference can cause problems, removing old ones doesn't seem to help TMD, and grinding someone's teeth to prevent TMD isn't supported. Don't build a new non-working contact into a crown, but don't grind away one that's always been there.

In short: sudden changes cause guarding, but people usually adapt once it's fixed. Joint instability has to be large, and needs heavy force, to matter. And an old, harmless problem can become a problem when the tolerance drops: the straw that broke the camel's back. A rule of thumb: trouble moving the jaw is usually the muscles; pain once the teeth are together is usually the joints.

Treatments

Occlusal therapy is anything that changes the bite. Reversible treatments: education, physical therapy, medication, counseling and a flat plane stabilization splint, the only one of these that changes the bite. Irreversible treatments: adjusting (grinding) the teeth, restorations, a repositioning splint, orthodontics, jaw surgery and joint surgery.

A splint is a plastic cover over the biting surfaces with a new, ideal bite built on it, so the joints can sit seated. It helps sore muscles, protects teeth and crowns, eases joint pain and works as a trial treatment. It is "hugely effective." A stabilizing splint keeps the joints seated; a repositioning splint holds the jaw in a different, chosen position (for some disc problems or sleep apnea). Other names: night guard, occlusal device or appliance, bite plate.

An upper splint has a flat back surface and a ramp in front. It's very stable, tough and easy to adjust, works for any bite class, and is best for a Class II division 1 bite with a big overjet; it's usually worn at night. A lower splint gets in the way of speech less and shows less, so it's better for daytime. Full coverage (all the teeth) is recommended almost always. Partial coverage can push covered teeth in and let uncovered teeth drift out, may work less well, and small ones can be swallowed at night.

Most irreversible dental work is just normal dentistry for broken or decayed teeth. But for a patient with a functional disturbance, do something permanent only when there's good reason to think the bite is the main cause, and do the least you can. How much depends on how far off the bite is: the rule of thirds. Within the first third of the tooth, adjust the enamel (remove first contacts, remove interferences, make forces go straight down, then perfect the bite; never into dentin). In the middle third, crowns and minor orthodontics. Beyond that, major orthodontics, jaw surgery and crowns.

Reversible and irreversible treatments have about the same long-term success, 50-90%, so start conservative, and go further only if that fails. Also weigh symptoms, the teeth's condition, health, looks and cost.

3. Trauma

"A force is only traumatic when it causes trauma." Five things decide that: how strong, how often, how long, which direction (sideways is worse than straight down) and how many teeth share it. Macrotrauma is a sudden big force, like a car crash; microtrauma is small repeated force, like grinding. Results include a broken jaw, joint damage and damage to teeth: cracks, looseness and wear. Inside, the ligament and bone around the tooth change; you see loose or drifting teeth, wear, a wider ligament space on x-ray, tenderness and tooth pain. Force damages the attachment around the root, rarely the gums.

Loose teeth

A healthy tooth doesn't visibly move up and down, but it does sink about 28 microns when you bite, front or back. It springs back about 7 microns right away and takes about 4 hours to fully recover. An implant moves only 2-3 microns under 10 pounds.

Side-to-side movement is always bigger. Single-root teeth move more than multi-root teeth. About 500 grams of push moves a tooth 56-108 microns; up to 150 microns is normal, more than that is not. Teeth are loosest when you wake up and tightest late in the day.

Adapted looseness stays the same and can last for years without harm. Traumatic looseness keeps getting worse, and that's when teeth are splinted together. You can only tell them apart by checking over time. Miller's index: 0 no movement, 1 barely noticeable, 2 sideways up to 1 mm, 3 more than 1 mm or pushing down or turning.

Worn teeth

Some wear is normal for age; the same wear at 30 isn't. Wear rarely hurts, so patients usually come in because of looks, often late. Treat it before it spreads to many teeth; the canines and front teeth that guide the jaw wear first. Badly worn teeth may need gum surgery, root canals or orthodontic pulling-up before crowns, unless 3 mm of tooth shows above the gum point between teeth.

The four kinds: attrition is tooth-on-tooth grinding (shiny, sharp-edged spots that match the opposite tooth); abrasion is wear from something in between, most often a toothbrush; erosion is acid (dull, cupped-out surfaces, with fillings left standing above the tooth); abfraction is the idea that flexing under bite force chips notches near the gumline. Acid speeds up the other kinds.

Acid patterns: reflux (GERD) erodes the tongue side of all the upper teeth and the tops of the lower molars, often worse on the side the person sleeps on. Bulimia mostly erodes the upper front teeth, and can destroy them while the lower front teeth are spared. Soda: swishing gives all-over satin erosion; holding it at the back is severe, with lots of cavities. Sucking lemons makes front teeth look like screwdriver tips. Also drugs, chlorinated pools and battery or galvanizing work.

Notches at the gumline (noncarious cervical lesions) are very common, more so with age, most often on the cheek side of upper premolars. They are rounded saucers or sharp V-notches, usually without decay. They're filled with composite only when needed (growing, sensitive, unsightly, trapping food). Their cause is mixed: hard sideways brushing, acid and reflux, with the bite involved but not enough on its own. Abfraction works in the lab but hasn't been proven in patients, so it isn't counted as a main type of wear. Clenching and nail biting are linked to these notches more than grinding is.

3 and 4. Stress and deep pain

Stress works through the brain's emotional centers, which tighten the muscle sensors (spindles) so muscles, especially in the head and neck, stay tense and hurt more easily. Deep pain (below the skin or gums) is easy to miss: a bad tooth can limit opening, and fixing the tooth brings the opening back. Neck pain can affect the jaw too.

5. Clenching, grinding and other habits

These habits are outside normal function and mostly unconscious, so they're hard to control. Daytime: clenching (look for chipped, broken or splayed teeth and bony bumps called tori), grinding, cheek or tongue biting, thumb sucking, odd postures, chewing pens or nails, holding a phone or violin under the chin. Nighttime: bruxism (rhythmic clenching and grinding in sleep), pushing the tongue against the teeth (a scalloped tongue edge), cheek biting.

Bruxism is very damaging: the forces are 3-5 times normal, sideways, in any jaw position, and the protective reflexes are off while you sleep. Sleep is about 80% non-REM and 20% REM. Grinding starts when sleep gets lighter; in sleep labs, lights or sounds can trigger it. Most events last 5-10 seconds, many times a night.

Bruxism starts in the brain, more like restless legs than a bite problem. It's linked to oxygen levels (sleep apnea), stress, medications and genes. The bite doesn't start it. The main treatment is a stabilization splint: grinding stops for a while, then comes back, so the point is to grind on the splint instead of the teeth ("the $400 splint instead of the $40,000 rehab"). Sleeping on your side, managing stress, less alcohol, quitting smoking, hypnosis and acupuncture are also suggested, with little proof.

Studies showed nighttime jaw muscle activity going up with stressful events (a job interview, a fight, quitting a job) and down on vacation, along with pain. That's why TMD care involves other health professionals.

Children often grind, usually without symptoms, as their changing teeth look for a stable bite. Tell parents it's usually harmless and to watch it; see a dentist if chewing is affected.

The big picture: the bite matters in a few of these problems, but most have nothing to do with it. Even so, a simple splint often helps them heal. It treats the symptoms, not the cause.
plain.dentures:
What's tested
  • Why denture "bite" is different: the goal is to keep a loose plate in the mouth, so balance means it doesn't tip
  • Support, stability and retention, and why stability (no sliding sideways) matters most
  • What holds a denture in: the thin film of saliva and the seal at the edges, a good fit, and most of all the patient's muscle control
  • How the bone shrinks after teeth are lost (upper jaw up and in, lower jaw down and out), and why dentures are often set in crossbite
  • The setups: balanced, non-balanced (also called neutrocentric) and lingualized, who gets which, and the table comparing them
  • Why a denture's bite is built and checked on an articulator, not in the mouth (Hanau's Realeff), and which of Thielemann's factors you can't change
  • Kinds of denture teeth, their cusp angles (30-33°, 12-22°, 0°) and how they're picked

This lecture (11/5) is about bites on dentures. The class hasn't had its denture course yet (it starts in January), so Dr. Givan explained what dentures are first. The big idea: for a denture, the bite's job is to keep the denture in the mouth and let the patient function. A full denture just sits on the gums, with nothing holding it. Patients who call them "plates" aren't far off: imagine a dinner plate trying to stay put in someone's mouth.

Denture words

Denture teeth aren't real teeth, just tooth-colored plastic. They sit in the pink denture base, which fits over the gums; the better it fits, the better it stays in. The edges that run up into the cheek and lip pocket are the flange, and the edge of the flange, where moving tissue meets tissue that doesn't move, is the peripheral border. Someone with no teeth is edentulous; they wear complete (or full) dentures. If some teeth are left, it's a partial denture.

When teeth are lost, the jawbone shrinks (resorption). Losing a lot makes eating very hard, especially with the lower denture. That problem is what led to dental implants about 50 years ago: to hold dentures in.

A short history

What did occlusion have to do with early dentures? "Practically none." (The history slides say "No test questions": know the point, not the dates.) The first ones were carved from wood or ivory, mostly for looks. Later ones had hinges or springs at the back, including Fauchard's (the father of dentistry), but you couldn't really eat or talk with them. George Washington's dentures weren't wooden: his dentist, John Greenwood, carved them from bone and ivory with gold bases and springs, and the Washingtons' letters (at UAB's Reynolds Historical Library) complain about the same soreness patients have today.

Later, dentures fit well enough to hold by suction (Gardette noticed that air pressure held a well-fitting base in). Porcelain came next: Duchâteau's porcelain dentures (about 1774) chipped and looked too white, and in 1808 Fonzi made single porcelain teeth that lasted in the mouth. Bonwill made the first real try at a denture bite: keep the teeth touching all the time so the denture stays in. That's why he's the "father of articulation." Old ideas about tooth shape stuck around: matching the patient's personality (molds are still called "bold" or "soft") and matching the face shape (square, tapered, ovoid). In the early 1900s Gysi, working with the company that became Dentsply, perfected balanced dentures; his Trubyte teeth are still sold. The point: a denture's bite is about not tipping, not about guiding forces the way it is with real teeth.

Why the denture bite is different

Without teeth, there's no feedback from the teeth and their ligaments, so patients only vaguely sense where they are. Think of a denture wearer as having one upper tooth and one lower tooth: each denture moves as one piece. So the teeth are arranged to keep the denture from tipping when they touch. That's what balance means: touching on both sides at once, so a chewing movement to the right doesn't flip the denture up on the left. Those balancing contacts are exactly what we avoid on natural teeth.

What holds a denture in

Suction and saliva help a well-fitting denture stick. The slides say what helps most: the thin film of saliva between the denture and the gums, and the pull of that film at the edges; suction, vacuum and stickiness help less. A good seal around the edges keeps air from leaking under it. All of it depends on the patient's saliva (it changes with age) and on a good fit, and chewing or a hot drink undoes most of it. The real key is the patient's muscle control: some people keep even bad dentures in and eat fine; others can't manage the best one. "Muscle control is likely to be the most important factor." Most of the day the teeth are apart, so those forces are what hold the denture then. Bony bulges (undercuts) help only a little and can make it sore, and a loose denture speeds up bone loss.

What makes it harder

What stops it tipping. Tall, wide ridges, a deep palate (a big help for the upper denture) and the right kind of seal at the back give the denture something to hold onto; so do an inner surface that fits the gums closely and teeth that touch without pushing the denture around. As bone is lost, it gets harder. A post dam (posterior palatal seal) at the back of an upper denture presses into the soft tissue to make up for the plastic shrinking; milled dentures often don't need one.

"All removable is movable." Dentures always move a little. The gums are soft and squish when the teeth bite, so the denture shifts. Hanau called this the Realeff ("resiliency and like effect"). That's why a denture's bite is built on an articulator, not in the mouth.

How the bone shrinks. The upper jaw shrinks up and in, so it gets smaller. The lower jaw shrinks down and out, so at tooth level it ends up bigger. Front upper: up and back (in). Back upper: up and toward the middle. Front lower: down and forward. Back lower: down and away from the middle (out). Because denture teeth go over the ridge, they're often set in crossbite, and that's fine.

Jaw sizes. Class I: the jaws match. Class II: the lower jaw is small and set back. Class III: the lower jaw is bigger and forward. When bone loss makes the lower jaw look bigger than the upper, it's a pseudo-Class III.

Also: the tongue gets bigger after teeth are lost, which mostly troubles the lower denture. And people whose teeth were just pulled aren't easier: there may not be enough room between the jaws for the denture.

Support, stability and retention

The three things to remember about any removable denture:

Support resists pushing down into the gums. The palate on top, and the cheek-side shelf and the pad behind the last tooth on the bottom, handle it well; the ridges themselves don't.

Retention resists being pulled off, like peanut butter pulling the denture loose, or the tongue lifting the lower one. Patients notice it most, but it doesn't hurt.

Stability resists sliding sideways. It's the most important: a denture that shifts when you bite really hurts, and patients can't eat. Implants are great at stability; even two can change a patient's life. We chew side to side, not straight up and down like a shark, which makes stability harder. The denture's bite helps most with stability. For support, the teeth should touch on both sides, evenly and at the same time, pushing the denture onto the ridges: flat teeth do it with a flat plane, cusped teeth by fitting cusp into groove.

Centric relation and centric occlusion

When a denture wearer bites, the muscles seat the jaw joints, so centric relation is easy to find. The teeth fitting together with the joints seated is called centric occlusion. We don't say MIP for dentures, because MIP is a position the nerves and muscles learn from real teeth. When the dentures close, usually only the back teeth touch; the front bone (premaxilla) doesn't handle force well, so the front teeth are mainly for looks.

The three setups

Balanced (also called bilateral balance or "anatomic" occlusion): the teeth touch when you close and in every sliding movement, on both sides at once. Definition: both sides, front and back teeth, touching at the same time in centric and eccentric positions. With tall-cusped teeth the front teeth can even touch when you slide forward. It needs a semi-adjustable articulator set up to match the patient (a facebow and a protrusive record), and skill.

Non-balanced (the slides also call it neutrocentric: flatten everything and keep the forces in the middle): the teeth touch only when you close; in any sliding movement they separate. Use flat (0°) teeth on a flat plane parallel to the ridges, no curve, no front-tooth contact, and set the articulator's condyle angle to zero, so the patient's own joint angle pulls the teeth apart as they move. Set the teeth as far toward the tongue as it allows, make them 40% narrower to ease the load on the ridge, keep them parallel to the denture bases (and tell the patient not to bite with the front teeth), use cuspless teeth, and maybe skip the lower second molars where the jaw starts curving up. Easy to set up.

Why does non-balanced work? While chewing, food sits between the teeth, so there's no balance anyway. Denture patients learn to chew on both sides, chew straight up and down, take small bites and chew with the premolars, not the front teeth. An old saying sums it up: "Enter bolus, exit balance."

Lingualized: the middle ground, and the one you'll probably use most. The upper teeth (semi-anatomic) have a long tongue-side cusp that works like a mortar and pestle against flat or wide-grooved lower teeth (0-12°), and the cheek-side cusps don't touch. It's easy to set and can be balanced (touching when you close and when you slide) or non-balanced (touching only when you close). Can the front teeth touch? In class he said never; the slides say not really, though it can be made up for. Pick non-balanced for a lot of bone loss, flabby gums, poor coordination or difficult jaw sizes; balanced for good ridges, firm gums and good coordination. Upsides, from the slides: the contacts move half a tooth toward the tongue, so the force lands over the ridge; one contact point; less rubbing; room for food to escape; simpler side-to-side contacts; and it works with any ridge, so for almost anyone. Downside: with fewer contacts it can wear faster and the bite can collapse a little.

The four setups compared. The slides rate them from − to +++. Balanced is best for looks (+++) and stability while chewing (++), but scores − on simple technique, easy records, low sideways force, easy adjusting, Class II and III jaws, and centered force. Balanced lingualized: + for looks, biting through food, stability while chewing and easy adjusting. Non-balanced lingualized: + for nearly everything, ++ for easy adjusting, − only for stability while chewing. Non-balanced: − for looks, biting through food and stability while chewing, but ++ for simple technique, easy records and low sideways force, +++ for easy adjusting, and + for Class II and III jaws and centered force.

Building balance

Rudolph Hanau, an engineer, made balance easier. He saw that the soft gums keep moving (the Realeff), so you can't build or mark a denture's bite in the mouth: with articulating paper, the denture tips and everything marks. It's done on an articulator, and fine-tuned by putting the dentures back on the articulator (a clinical remount), never by grinding in the mouth. His balanced dentures also had heavy contacts on the first molars to make up for the squishy gums and joints. He tied the five factors together (Hanau's quint), and Thielemann's formula (spelled Thielmann in the Review lecture) shows the math: steepen the plane, for example, and you flatten the curve or the cusps to keep the teeth touching. For dentures we use them to keep teeth together; for natural teeth, to keep them apart. Two factors are fixed: the jaw joint's angle, and the plane of the teeth, lined up with the eyes and with Camper's line from the nose to the ear (it changes only a little). Three can vary: the front-teeth guidance (rarely used, since the front teeth usually don't touch), the curve and the cusp angle. So balance comes from the curve, the cusp angle and a little plane. To set up balance, the joint angle comes from a forward-bite record.

Denture teeth

Porcelain: the best looking and barely wears, so it keeps the bite height, but it can chip, it's hard to set and adjust, it clicks, and it doesn't bond to the base, so it's held with pins (front teeth) or holes with undercuts (back teeth). Composite and cross-linked plastic: the most common, what most good dentures use; layered for a natural look, doesn't chip, quieter, easy to adjust and polish, bonds to the base, costs more. It still wears: in 5-7 years the back teeth wear into a reverse curve and chew poorly. Acrylic: cheap, bonds, easy to shape and can be ground down to fit a tight space, but wears and stains; mostly for temporary dentures. Worn denture teeth let the bite close down, so wear resistance matters.

Picking the teeth

Teeth come in matched sets from a mold chart. You pick the upper front mold, and the chart tells you the lower front mold and the back teeth for each setup. So "the denture occlusion is entirely based upon" that upper front mold, and it's picked mostly for looks: "soft" or "bold," square, tapering or ovoid.

Helpful guides: the wax rim tried in the mouth shows lip support, where the front edges go, the midline, where the canines go, and the plane the teeth are set to. Old rules of thumb, like the front tooth being about 1/16 of the cheekbone-to-cheekbone width (Berry, 1906) or measuring across the nose, aren't scientific, but they tend to look good. The back teeth depend on the setup and on the patient's muscle control, ridges, jaw sizes, the room between the jaws, and whether they've worn dentures before (everyone starts over with new ones). Pick a natural shade, not "headlights." Denture teeth are usually a bit smaller than real ones. For the back teeth the slides check six things: a color that matches the front teeth, narrower than natural teeth, a height that fits the room between the jaws and matches the canine, a length that runs from behind the canine to the pad at the back of the ridge, the cusp angle, and the material.

Tooth shapes. Anatomic teeth have tall cusps (30-33°), look the most natural, allow balance, resist the denture rotating and spread the load, but need more records, setup and skill, push the denture sideways more, are hard to fine-tune, and their results don't last as the denture settles and cheap ones wear. Semi-anatomic teeth (also called functional or anatoline) have lower cusps (about 12-22°); the front teeth can't touch unless the plane or curve makes up for it. Flat teeth (0°, also called cuspless, zero-degree, rational, flat-plane or monoline) push the denture sideways the least, suit any jaw size and crossbites, are easy to adjust and suit patients with poor muscle control; but they cut food poorly (more pressure on the ridges), are hard to balance and some patients don't like them.

What the evidence says

Tall-cusped teeth look best and chew a little better, but flat, non-balanced dentures work just as well for patients, who stay well fed. Chewing is just one factor in choosing. Most patients want to smile at their grandkids and enjoy a meal. A 2013 review the slides cite (Abduo) found patients prefer cusped teeth set balanced or lingualized over flat non-balanced ones, though the research isn't conclusive and every setup generally works.

Partial dentures

The more teeth lost, the more you think like a full denture (keep it stable). The more teeth left, the more you think like natural teeth (canine guidance or group function, back teeth separating), because the teeth are in charge. Implants add more to think about, and every removable denture moves a little.

The big picture: a denture's bite is about keeping it in the mouth. Each denture works as one piece, balance means it doesn't tip, and stability matters most.
plain.nccl:
What's tested
  • Cavities vs notches at the gumline: the same spot, a different cause
  • The three causes of the notches, alone or together: brushing, biting forces and acid
  • Brushing: the toothpaste matters more than the brush; the RDA number; soft brushes, less pressure; worse on the side of the hand you brush with
  • Why not every notch comes from brushing
  • Biting forces (abfraction): how a push on the biting surface makes a notch at the neck of the tooth, its clues and the night guard
  • Acid: erosion vs cavities, where throwing up does damage, pH vs buffering capacity, and the worst drinks
  • Fix the cause, and when to fill a notch

This lecture is Dr. Lawson's, recorded ahead of time for the 11/12 class. It's about noncarious cervical lesions (NCCLs): notches worn into a tooth at the gumline that aren't cavities.

Cavity or not?

Plaque collects at the gumline, so cavities form there too. Those look like cavities: soft and brown, and a good filling for them is resin-modified glass ionomer. NCCLs sit in the same spot but have a different cause: not decay. There are three causes, and a notch can have one, two or all three:

  • Abrasion: from brushing.
  • Abfraction: from biting forces.
  • Erosion: from acid.

Brushing (abrasion)

A researcher (Dzakovich) brushed pulled teeth set in fake gums and made notches like the real ones near the gum line. Brushing without toothpaste made no notches, so the toothpaste matters more than the brush. Ask what toothpaste the patient uses.

A toothpaste's RDA (relative dentin abrasivity) says how scratchy it is: a higher number means more abrasive. Pick a low one. (A Colgate whitening paste is about 124; Crest Pro-Health is always high.)

Still use a soft brush: it protects the gums too. Brush with less pressure; an electric toothbrush with a pressure sensor helps. A clue: people press harder on the side of the hand they brush with, so brushing notches are worse on that side. Notches only on the left? Ask if the patient is left-handed.

Not every notch is from brushing

People with leprosy who couldn't brush their own teeth, ancient people from before toothbrushes, and animals (a camel, a cat) have had these notches. They also show up on the roof of the mouth, where people don't brush, and under the gums, where bristles can't reach. So something else causes some of them.

Biting forces (abfraction)

A push on the slope of a cusp bends the tooth to one side. The tooth is held in the bone, which acts as the pivot. Teeth, like most materials, handle squeezing better than stretching. The side being stretched is under tension, and that's where the notch forms, just above the bone. Think of pushing on a stop sign: it bends at the ground, and the stretched side is where it gets damaged.

It's hard to tell for sure, but clues are bony bumps (tori and exostoses) and worn, matching spots on the teeth from grinding. The fix: a night guard, a piece of plastic to grind on instead of the teeth (here it isn't a treatment for jaw joint problems). Dr. Givan's L7 adds that abfraction is shown in the lab but not yet proven in patients.

Acid (erosion)

Cavities are acid too, but made by bacteria where plaque sits. Erosion is acid from what we eat, drink or bring up, wherever the liquid sits. Cupped-out molar tips come from wear plus acid: once the enamel wears through and the dentin underneath shows, the acid eats the dentin faster, because dentin starts to dissolve at a higher pH than enamel. Throwing up erodes the tongue side of the upper teeth: the lip protects the outside surfaces, and the tongue covers the lower teeth.

Drinks

Talk to patients about acidic drinks, and explain pH simply (water is 7; lower is more acidic). Milk in coffee makes it less acidic, and tea beats coffee. In sparkling water, more bubbles means more acid; the flavor doesn't matter.

Buffering capacity is how much saliva (bicarbonate) it takes to neutralize a drink. Needing more is worse. pH is read with a probe; buffering capacity is measured by adding bicarbonate bit by bit until the pH is back to neutral. Measured that way, orange juice and wine are much worse than their pH alone suggests. Citric acid grabs calcium (it's a chelator), so citrus is very erosive. Safer choices: water, milk, or Milo's sweet tea (no fermentable sugar if it's made with Splenda).

Raising the pH

Mouth rinses can be acidic, but you don't rinse for long, so he isn't worried about them. To raise the mouth's pH, use a base: bicarbonate, as in a baking soda rinse or Basic Bites candies (bicarbonate plus arginine). Rinsing with water, keeping acidic drinks to mealtimes and using a straw make sense but aren't proven. Water doesn't neutralize much: pH is a log scale, so you'd need a swimming pool of it. A base works.

Fix the cause, then decide on a filling

Find the cause first: someone who sucks on lemons all day doesn't need a toothpaste talk. Brushing: a lower-RDA toothpaste, then a pressure-sensor brush. Acid: a less acidic drink and bicarbonate. Biting forces: a night guard.

You don't have to fill a notch that is easy to keep clean, doesn't hurt, looks fine and isn't deep (near the nerve). One that fails any of those gets filled.
